title: Perhaps Connecting Fridges to the Internet Was a Bad Idea
excerpt: Bags of frozen blueberries and Swedish meatballs, packets of waffles and pizzas, and tub after tub of ice cream: all melted, floppy, spoiled, and stinking
body: Bags of frozen blueberries and Swedish meatballs, packets of waffles and pizzas, and tub after tub of ice cream: all melted, floppy, spoiled, and stinking
This has been the scene at grocery stores across Europe after their fridges and freezers have been hacked
Last month, employees at hundreds of supermarkets in France came into work to find they had to trash millions of dollars’ worth of food
The machines were not simply deactivated; they had been remotely hijacked and reprogrammed to hit temperatures as high as 122 degrees Fahrenheit
Last Monday, grocery outlets in at least seven more countries, including Estonia, Belgium, and Sweden, experienced a near-identical incident
The same day, freezers at the French national blood bank were also hacked (though staffers were able to intervene before any samples were corrupted)

Depending on who you talk with, America is either next or has already been hit: In August, the Pentagon quietly revealed that freezers at commissaries on several U.S. military bases had malfunctioned in a suspected attack
No one has claimed responsibility for any of these exploits, and it’s not even clear whether they are connected
The hackers seemingly didn’t have a goal besides sowing chaos and wasting an enormous amount of food
Perhaps the most surprising aspect of these widespread fridge attacks is that they haven’t happened sooner
For hackers, these appliances make perfect targets
The basic problem is that many fridges and freezers are now connected to the internet. “The attacks are very simple,” Nadiya Kostyuk, a cybersecurity researcher at Carnegie Mellon University, told me
Each unit has a microcontroller that is connected to the local network, so even someone sitting at a computer thousands of miles away can theoretically access it

These devices are typically password protected, but they still tend to be pretty easy to crack, Kostyuk explained. “Usually it’s done by brute force,” which is to say the devices are spammed with password after password until one works
Some of the recent attacks were made simpler because usernames and passwords had never been changed from the manufacturer’s defaults

Once the hackers remotely broke into a system, they were able to take control of a heating element that can be periodically switched on to prevent frost from building up on the evaporator coils, which stops the freezer from working as effectively
Instructed to run repeatedly, that heating element has proved capable of cooking perishable food

For a home fridge, the benefits—a touchscreen that can show family photos, an interior camera so you can see what you already have while you’re at the grocery store—may not outweigh the security risks

In the aftermath of the recent attacks, people have assumed the same is true for industrial fridges: Why on earth does a supermarket fridge need to be online? But for the millions of supermarket chill cabinets, refrigerated trucks and shipping containers, and gigantic cold-storage warehouses that our food sits in on its way from farm to table, the calculus is quite different

Logistics companies are often required to demonstrate that food has stayed within a narrow temperature range while in their custody; the ability for a freezer to broadcast an alert if its temperature deviates from a set point at 2 a.m. is an extremely useful feature

Refrigeration units are always on—they have to run 24/7 by design—and a lot of today’s smartest devices provide the diagnostics that allow companies to perform predictive maintenance to preempt any potential issues. “The risk of loss is so high if the unit goes down,” Chris Gaffney, a supply-chain expert at Georgia Tech who previously ran logistics for Coca-Cola, told me
The food that our fridges are protecting is extremely fragile; the machines themselves are quite complex; and qualified technicians are in short supply
A refrigerated warehouse, let alone a supermarket, won’t have a person with that kind of specialist skill set on-site, Gaffney said
But when connected to the internet, a scattered portfolio of freezers can be managed and sometimes even fixed remotely

And, as politicians push legislation to make food traceable, the entire supply chain is being digitized. “There are a lot of positives that come with that—ways to increase our food security and understanding where food is coming from,” Sara Stickler, the president of the Global Cold Chain Alliance, an industry trade group, told me. “But with digitization, there also comes risks.” The food business isn’t like banking, where online security is central to a company’s value proposition

In perishable logistics, where the mission is keeping food cold, warehouse operators and grocery stores have not typically seen the value in spending extra on cybersecurity. “Margins are tough,” Gaffney said

When it comes to adopting sophisticated new technology, he told me, “logistics is a laggard, and within logistics, cold is a laggard.” The genius and horror of hacking refrigeration is that although the cold chain is essential infrastructure, it’s not treated as such
As I quickly learned while writing Frostbite , my recent book on the topic, almost no one has a complete picture of refrigeration’s scope and scale
Nearly three-quarters of everything on the American plate passes through the cold chain on its way to our tables

Thousands of chilled warehouses, refrigerated containers and trucks, meat lockers, and banana-ripening rooms are located out of sight, underground, at ports, near freeway intersections or cattle ranches: Added together, these pockets of artificial winter form the invisible backbone of our food system

Meanwhile, refrigeration is somehow different from other crucial infrastructure—water-treatment plants, say, or power stations—where the public may be ignorant, but at least industry members and government officials are on top of how many facilities we have and where they are

As supermarket shelves emptied during the early days of COVID, one industry expert told me that he received a frantic call from a senior official in the government asking how many refrigerated trucks and warehouses the country’s food supply depended on
If there is a silver lining to these attacks, it is that they could serve as a wake-up call. “With these cyberattacks, it totally redefines what ‘critical infrastructure’ is,” Kostyuk said

After all, cyberattacks are not the only threat facing our food-supply chain: Dozens of supermarket refrigerators across the U.K. failed this summer during a heatwave that pushed them beyond their limits, and severe-weather-induced blackouts are a constant threat
Whether the culprit is a hacker or the weather, the outcome remains the same
Get used to seeing more empty supermarket shelves.

title: On SNL , the Struggle (For Power) Was Real
excerpt: This season of Saturday Night Live has gotten a lot of mileage from inaction
body: This season of Saturday Night Live has gotten a lot of mileage from inaction

Week after week, sketch after sketch—as James Austin Johnson’s version of Donald Trump interrupts whatever comedy might be at play—the show’s performers have done more than merely step aside as the president storms the stage
Instead, his presence leaves them comically petrified: frozen, at pretty much the moment of his entrance, unable to do anything else

Like much of what plays out on live TV, the gag works because, so often, it doesn’t quite; half the fun is watching stars such as Kenan Thompson, temporarily transformed into audience members, trying to stifle their laughter while Johnson Trumps it up
The freeze-frame device also works, though, because of its upstager in chief
Few jokes capture the president’s scene-stealing capabilities better than ones that find Trump like a modern-day Medusa, turning everyone in his path to stone
There’s a fine line, however, between running joke and crutch—and it’s one that SNL has frequently crossed
Only five episodes into the current season, the freeze-frame bits have become notably tepid
But on last night’s episode, the freeze frames were not just the point; they made a point
The cold open was an inevitable recap of the midterm elections: the blue wave that, on Tuesday, swept the country

The sketch’s action began in expected fashion, with the Senate Democrats Hakeem Jeffries (played by Thompson) and Chuck Schumer (Sarah Sherman) celebrating, and analyzing, their party’s landslide victory
How did they do it? What was the source of their historic rebuke to Trump, the MAGA coalition, and the political status quo? “ Me !” said Trump, storming the stage
Johnson’s version of the president blathered (about Millennial cringe, about the long-gone sitcom New Girl , about men’s backsides); Colin Jost, as Pete Hegseth, at one point smarmed onto the scene
All along, Jeffries and Schumer were relegated to the background, present but vacant: two power players rendered awkwardly inert
The staging made sense—because the up staging made sense
The sketch, dominated by Trump even in his moment of loss, hinted at Democrats’ famed ability to snatch defeat from the jaws of victory
It also visualized the fickle workings of American party politics
Power, particularly in this moment, is largely a function of attention: a matter of which politician can occupy the forefront of voters’ screens and minds
The sketch, as each character jockeyed for eyeballs, managed to turn that reality into comedy
American politics is a battle of attrition; last night, on SNL , the (power) struggle was real
The episode’s host made that opening salvo especially apt

The comedian Druski has made a specialty out of skewering the politics of race (which he brought with him to the show, including to a sketch co-starring Andrew Dismukes as a fictional Atlantic reporter) and rose to fame posting comedy videos to Instagram
He is the first digital creator to host SNL
His episode’s cold open fittingly, and elegantly, mimicked the workings of the phone screen and the brute dynamics of the digital economy
Images, vying for primacy: That’s how information works now
Candidates battle not just to convince voters that their way is the right way but also to simply be there, crowding out the other contenders—undeniable, unavoidable, and ever in the foreground
The sketch, in recognition of that, anointed a new scene stealer: Senator-Elect James Talarico, whose victory this week helped turn Texas blue
Operating in another long-standing SNL tradition, Talarico made a surprise cameo, closing out the sketch by upstaging everyone else, literally and symbolically

The lame-duck executive, the leaders of the legislative establishment—for the first time in a long time, they were relegated to the background as the young politician talked about a new day in American politics. “It’s clear people want something new,” Talarico announced, grinning, as SNL ’s live audience whooped in approval
But true change—real transformation—is more easily scripted than done
And before Talarico shouted the customary “Live from New York” tagline, he ended his appearance with a joke that, ironically but perhaps appropriately, upstaged his own message
Americans want something different, he said, before getting to the punch line: “I’m talking, of course, about SNL ’s cold opens.”

title: The Democrats’ Fight Over Israel Is Just Beginning
excerpt: D uring a swing through Detroit in the final days of the midterm campaign, former President Obama invoked the kind of gauzy pluralism that Democrats were so pro
body: D uring a swing through Detroit in the final days of the midterm campaign, former President Obama invoked the kind of gauzy pluralism that Democrats were so proud of during his presidency

He pointed out that Michigan had the opportunity to pull off an improbable feat: By electing Abdul El-Sayed to join Elissa Slotkin in the Senate, the state could turn its delegation into a walking symbol of buried enmities and transcendent harmony. “You’ve got a Muslim man, you’ve got a Jewish woman fighting for you in the United States Senate,” Obama said. “That’s something, Michigan, you can be proud of.” It took exactly a week for that optimism to run aground on the rougher shoals of modern Democratic politics

The following Sunday, Representative Haley Stevens withdrew her backing of El-Sayed and threw it to his opponent, the Republican Mike Rogers, citing, in part, El-Sayed’s stance on the issue that has divided Democrats more than any other this year: Israel
The abrupt reversal didn’t prevent El-Sayed from winning decisively

But that outcome masked the apprehensions that I heard again and again this week from Michigan Democrats about the potential for tensions over the Middle East to rupture the broad coalition that the party assembled to win in 2026
By the time I sat down with a group of Democratic activists at a red-sauce joint in Ann Arbor, on Election Night, the first bottle of wine was already empty
Nearly everyone at the table had voted for El-Sayed, who, hours later, would go on to make history as the first Muslim elected to the U.S

If anything, the Jewish Democrats sharing bruschetta and pasta seemed a little shell-shocked, groggily emerging from a bitter Senate campaign and reckoning with what they described as one of the most difficult votes they had ever cast
Rubini Naidu for The Atlantic Annie Wolock, Cindy Bank, and Beth Bashert gathered on Election Night in Ann Arbor, Michigan
Everyone at the table wanted the same thing: to see Democrats retake control of the Senate and repudiate President Trump

None of them, however, was particularly excited to elect a senator who seeks to make Israel a pariah, who speaks about Zionism in a way that they said makes Michigan Jews unsafe, and who campaigned with Hasan Piker, the far-left streamer who has said that “America deserved 9/11.” In other words: They did not want to elect a senator like the candidate whom all but two of the people around the table had just voted for. “It’s hard to express the depth of heartache that’s happening here on the ground,” Decky Alexander, who organized the dinner of 11 people, told me
A theater professor, a vice chair of the state Democratic Party, and the leader of its Jewish caucus, Alexander voted for El-Sayed with certitude but not excitement
She views the far right as more of a problem to the country—and to American Jews—and her husband, Bruce Kutinsky, believes that the far left is a bigger threat

He reluctantly voted for Rogers, the Republican. [ Read: The Hasan Piker question ] Even as the group eagerly discussed the anticipated Democratic gains nationwide, there was a plaintive quality to their conversation about El-Sayed’s impending victory
Earlier that evening, the Ann Arbor–school–board member Rima Mohammad had none of that apprehension as she reflected on the Senate race outside a polling place across the street from Michigan Stadium
The 46-year-old pharmacist spoke softly, her voice scratchy after a long weekend of get-out-the-vote efforts

Mohammad, a Palestinian American whose grandparents were forcibly displaced from their homes in what is now Israel, in 1948, came to Ann Arbor for a residency at the University of Michigan, where she now teaches
Mohammad grew up poor in Cincinnati, part of the only family of color in a very conservative neighborhood
She told me that a victory by El-Sayed would be “life-changing,” especially for her four kids to see. “It’s not even about being Muslim,” Mohammad explained

A win would show that “elections are not gonna be bought” by corporations and groups such as AIPAC, she said, and “also that hate is not going to win.” The Israeli-Palestinian conflict has been perhaps the biggest and ugliest point of division within the Democratic Party in the three years since the October 7 Hamas attacks on Israel and the resulting war in Gaza

President Biden, a self-proclaimed Zionist who viewed Israel as both an essential security partner to the U.S. and a country with similar values, pledged American support for the war against Hamas—prompting a backlash by progressive activists
A protest movement led to more than 100,000 Democrats voting “uncommitted” in Michigan’s 2024 presidential primary to register their discontent
President Trump received more votes than Kamala Harris in Dearborn, the heart of Michigan’s Arab American community, which historically votes for Democrats
Rubini Naidu for The Atlantic McDonald Elementary School in Dearborn, Michigan Rubini Naidu for The Atlantic Rima Mohammad is running for Ann Arbor’s school board
This year, the Democratic Senate primary in Michigan became the main battleground for the party’s internal fight over the U.S. relationship with Israel
Stevens defended Israel as an “imperfect” ally, one that is America’s “truest friend” in the Middle East
El-Sayed has made clear that he does not view Israel as an American partner

He called the country “bloodthirsty” and said that, like Iran, it is a threat to the United States—rhetoric that some Jewish Michiganders worry might open the door to anti-Semitic elements on the left
After El-Sayed won the primary and Stevens backed him, the issue faded and the party appeared to be united, particularly amid Republicans’ overtly Islamophobic attacks on El-Sayed
Stevens’s last-second pivot to Rogers resurfaced an issue that Democrats will not be able to ignore for much longer
Democrats who are about to be in control of Congress now need to figure out how to handle divisions over Israel and Gaza that show no signs of being mended

There will be a “real battle for the soul of the party” as a number of Israel critics arrive in Washington, David Kramer, an insurance executive who served as chair of Stevens’s primary campaign, told me
El-Sayed is already talking about the issue

In his victory speech late Tuesday, he spoke about protecting Palestinian children from “being murdered by our tax dollars” and said that Michiganders “don’t want our money sent to do apartheid or genocide or war.” He took a moment to taunt AIPAC: “Thank you for giving me the opportunity to beat you twice.” J ewish and Muslim voters alike told me this week that they see El-Sayed’s election as a pivotal moment in Democrats’ evolution on the once-marginal issue of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict

Democrats have indisputably moved left over the course of the Gaza war; all but seven Democratic senators voted earlier this year to block certain weapons transfers to Israel, a tally that would have once been unthinkable. (Republicans, though still more reliably pro-Israel than Democrats, have also shifted away.) The question is whether El-Sayed will succeed in moving Democrats even further to the left, or whether the party, with a slew of new lawmakers and a surprisingly large Senate majority, will be able to find room for a wide spectrum of beliefs. [ Read: The anti-Democrat ] Many Muslim officials and activists see El-Sayed’s election as a banner moment for pro-Palestine activism

On Tuesday morning, outside a 100-year-old redbrick elementary school in Dearborn that served as a polling place for many in the city’s large Arab American community, Alabas Farhat sprinkled his good morning s with Arabic phrases as he greeted voters

The 26-year-old state representative from Dearborn said he cared less about El-Sayed being the first Muslim senator than about him being an “‘America First,’ ‘Michigan First’ U.S. senator.” El-Sayed maintains that Washington’s financial support for Israel’s war in Gaza—which left tens of thousands dead after Hamas militants attacked Israel in 2023 and killed approximately 1,200 people—means less tax money is available for health care and education back home in America
The message resonates for Farhat, whose family is from southern Lebanon. “He’s going to speak out when something is wrong in a way that the status quo will not know how to handle,” Farhat told me
Rubini Naidu for The Atlantic State Representative Alabas Farhat El-Sayed understands that Democrats’ attitudes toward Israel have shifted

In a June AP/NORC poll, 58 percent said that the U.S. was too supportive of Israel, up from 45 percent in early 2024; 62 percent of Democrats said that the U.S. was not supportive enough of Palestinians

title: Look Closer: A Mysterious Pair of Mittens
excerpt: Index of American Design / National Gallery of Art The mittens were almost 80 years old when Ethel Dougan painted this watercolor, one of more than 18,000 works
body: Index of American Design / National Gallery of Art The mittens were almost 80 years old when Ethel Dougan painted this watercolor, one of more than 18,000 works by some 1,000 financially strapped artists commissioned by the Index of American Design
Part of the Works Progress Administration’s Federal Art Project, the Index aimed to document historical American arts and crafts and provide inspiration for modern designers
The mittens had been knitted by the fiancée of Private Franklin Martin Spaulding, an 18-year-old who had enlisted in the 6th Massachusetts Volunteer Infantry Regiment in August 1862
He had seen active service through that winter, as had his mittens
The black-and-white photograph archived with Dougan’s drawing shows little more than a gray pile of moth-eaten wool
Her watercolor—now in the National Gallery of Art’s collection with the rest of the Index—brings the mittens back to life
Worn and faded, certainly, they are nonetheless spirited, with a patriotic color scheme, embroidered stars, and rib-stitched stripes
Arranged on the page with fingertips touching, they seem to reach toward each other like children holding hands
Dougan depicted the seams and rows with enough precision that an experienced knitter could re-create the design, but even a casual observer might note the mittens’ odd silhouette
Nestled between the usual two pouches—a big one for the fingers and a small one for the thumb—is a third
It’s there for the teenage soldier’s index finger, so he could tear the end off a paper cartridge, load his rifle, and pull the trigger in the cold
This article appears in the December 2026 print edition with the headline “Mittens.”

title: Can Beauty Make Us Good?
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube What is beauty? Is it really “in the eye of the beholder,” or is it an objective quality that exists in the w
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube What is beauty? Is it really “in the eye of the beholder,” or is it an objective quality that exists in the world? Is it a mere decorative feature of life, or does it have something important to tell us? These are enduring human questions, but ones that the art world and the academic humanities—the natural custodians of beauty—gave up answering for a long time
In this episode, David Brooks talks to the Harvard professor Elaine Scarry, whose now-classic book On Beauty and Being Just brought the subject back to serious attention 25 years ago
David and Scarry discuss the ladder of loves, the universal appeal of symmetry, and why even prisoners at Guantánamo want to look at pretty pictures
The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: Today’s episode is about beauty
The basic thesis of this show is that in our society, we have massive forces of dehumanization trying to shrink us and beleaguered forces of humanization
Nothing could be more humanizing than beauty

We’re going to talk about how to cultivate a taste for beauty, how to create beauty, and we’re going to entertain the question: Does experiencing beauty make you a better person? My conversation partner today is Elaine Scarry, a very eminent literature professor, a humanist
She has a fancy title here at Harvard University, the Walter M
Cabot Professor of Aesthetics and the General Theory of Value, which is a fantastic professor title
Elaine wrote a very important book in 1999 called On Beauty and Being Just
It was an important moment because there was an assault on beauty and the very idea of beauty striking through the academy, through the art world
We should shock people into improving society
We should create ugly things to shock them
In 1999, Elaine rose up to defend beauty, and I would say 26 years later, she has carried the day
Beauty is back on the agenda in the academy, in the artistic world
You may notice that we are not at our usual set at Yale University today
I want to reassure you that our podcast will not only be visiting colleges with gigantic endowments
I just happen to have a talk in Boston, so we thought we’d take advantage
I’m David Brooks, and this is The Permanent Questions
Brooks: Elaine Scarry, welcome to The Permanent Questions
Today we’re gonna talk about beauty, which you have—I don’t know if you’ve single-handedly rescued it in the academy, but you’ve done your part
I have to confess to you: I am an aesthetic Philistine
I recall when I wrote my first book, which was published in 2000, I wrote it in a dank, unfinished basement of my home with mildew and the smell of mildew everywhere
My desk was a plywood board, and my chair was a folding chair, and it was just me and my little laptop, and I was oblivious
A lot of people were like, “I’m not working here.” But even I occasionally have these moments when you’re undone by something tremendously beautiful
I think the thing that strikes you about them is they lift you out of everyday reality for at least a brief time
You’ve done so much work on beauty; you must have had encounters of that sort with beauty

I think that over time, the longer one lives, the more encounters one has, not just because they can keep accumulating and adding up, but because one learns to see or one becomes aware of just the astonishing plenitude that’s all around one
A kind of interesting analogy is what happens with color vision
John Dewey says that if you give small children the chance to learn color, it usually takes several years to be able to reliably identify a color
Whereas now researchers say that as adults, the average number of colors we can all see is 26,000, and if you count gray tones, it’s closer to a million
I think that something like that happens with beauty
You may not be aware of it as a child, or it may be happening to you, but you don’t have words for it
At one time, he was reading The Tale of Genji for about 20 minutes each morning
When he would begin to read, Lady Murasaki’s writing immediately lights up your mind
I would see pools of color that weren’t even directly prompted by what was said on the page
She’s writing about the court in Japan, but at the same time, Genji is always discovering beauty anywhere, in the outskirts and among poor people, and so forth
That kind of experience with reading is one that I’m sure we both have
Brooks: When you mentioned the ability to perceive more colors, there’s a neuroscientist at Northeastern named Lisa Feldman Barrett, who has a concept of emotional granularity
She says that some people can only experience very crude emotional categories

title: Why animals are smarter than we think
excerpt: When I was growing up, one of my favorite things to hear from an adult was that I was smart
body: When I was growing up, one of my favorite things to hear from an adult was that I was smart

It made me feel special — like I was capable of doing things that other people weren’t.  In hindsight, that pride came with baggage: pressure to do well academically, and a sense of competition that wasn’t always necessary

But many people in power still have a preoccupation with intelligence and conventional ways of measuring it.  Now, though, the way that we think about intelligence and markers of it, such as IQ, are shifting in important ways

David Robson, the author of The Intelligence Trap: Why Smart People Make Dumb Mistakes , says that traditional markers like IQ are not the only factors when considering how smart someone is. “There’s practical intelligence, which is much more about how good you are at planning projects and executing those projects,” he explains
He even says that people with high IQs tend to be more susceptible to things like confirmation bias
Philosopher Jeff Sebo goes further, arguing  that even focusing our discussion of intelligence on people is too narrow

He’s the author of the book The Moral Circle: Who Matters, What Matters, and Why , and he says that making humans the bar for intelligence is a mistake. “Intelligence in general is the ability to process information and solve problems and adapt to the environment,” he told Vox

Animals’ brains “might not look exactly like ours, but they can help animals solve problems and navigate their environments and adapt to their situations really effectively.” So what does animal intelligence actually look like? And what can we learn from it? We answer that and more on this week’s episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.  Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Sebo, edited for length and clarity
You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts
If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545

What is it about one animal’s intelligence that makes us want to protect it versus another animal that can end up on our dinner table? I think of dogs versus cows and pigs or dolphins versus fish.  There are many factors that shape how much empathy we have for non-human animals of various kinds

Are they cute and do they look like us? Do they remind us of ourselves? What role do we assign them in our lives?  We have more empathy by default for animals who play companion roles in our lives as opposed to animals who play commodity roles in our lives

This is why we can often have much more empathy for some animals over others, even if they display the same markers of sentience and the same markers of intelligence.  What’s a discovery about an animal’s mind that might surprise people? That might make us think of that animal differently than we maybe do?  There are really interesting studies showing that bees are capable of play behaviors
You can go online and see a video of a bee rolling a wooden ball around in a way that displays all the hallmarks of play activity

This is done seemingly for the pure joy of rolling a wooden ball around.  Likewise, there are studies showing that animals like insects have remarkable capacities for perception and learning and memory and adaptive, flexible decision-making and communication with each other
Animals that we might have written off as simple, as mechanistic, are in fact incredibly complex, seemingly sensitive, seemingly intelligent
I think that has allowed people to have a little bit more empathy for some of these animals than they otherwise might

How much of what we call animal intelligence is actually just animals doing the things that people happen to be good at? What kind of abilities are we overlooking when we think of animals and intelligence?  We do tend to look for markers of intelligence that we associate with human intelligence and that can sometimes lead us to overlook markers of specifically non-human intelligence
This can happen in so many different ways.  For example, for many years, the gold standard for self-awareness tests was a mirror self-recognition test

You would put a mark on the forehead of an animal and place them in front of a mirror and see if they notice the mark and if they try to remove the mark and that can signal a certain kind of self-awareness.  It took us a long time to appreciate that this might not be the best way to test self-awareness in many animals for a variety of reasons
Many animals are not primarily visual, so we might need to think about how to perform this kind of test with their sensory modalities

Also, many animals might not particularly care about whether they have a mark on their forehead, so we should probably not treat an attempt to remove that mark as a standard for self-awareness.  We hear that pigs are intelligent or that octopuses could solve puzzles and we think, “Oh wow, we should be treating these creatures better.” I wonder, is there a problem with that argument? Because what happens to the animals that just never impress us? I think that learning more about animal intelligence and challenging our preconceived notions about animals is good, but I think it would be a mistake to treat a certain level of intelligence — and especially a certain level of human-like intelligence — as a necessary condition for moral consideration.  That might lead us to extend respect and kindness to elephants and chimpanzees and other relatively human-like animals while neglecting the other animals who are conscious and sentient, capable of feelings and emotions, and that have forms of agency and decision-making, even if it might not look like ours
I think that bar should be lower and should at the very least include consciousness and sentience
This is making me realize that I may not be clear on what it means to be sentient

How do we know if an animal’s sentient or not?  This is very difficult to know for sure, because sentience is the capacity for positive and negative experiences like pleasure, pain, happiness, and suffering
The only experiences that any of us can directly experience are our own.  With non-human animals, we can collect behavioral evidence, internal evidence, developmental evolutionary evidence

For example, behaviorally, we can ask, “Do they nurse their own wounds? Do they respond to analgesics and antidepressants the way that we do?” And then developmentally, evolutionarily, we can ask, “In their ancestral environments, did they face pressures that they could overcome if they developed the ability to experience pleasure, pain, happiness, and suffering?” None of this is proof, none of it establishes certainty, but when we find a lot of this evidence in an animal, that at least increases the probability
In terms of ethics and policy, what matters is we should not wait for certainty that someone can suffer before taking basic steps to address welfare risks for them

If there is at least a realistic possibility that someone can suffer based on the evidence, then we should take reasonable proportionate steps to mitigate welfare risks for them when we make decisions that affect them.  I personally don’t think of plants as sentient, but one of the things I love about my monstera is whenever it’s moved around in my apartment, it turns itself towards the sun
Does it make sense to call them intelligent when they do things like that?  At least in a certain broad sense, I think that it does

Many plants have capacities for perception, for collecting information from the environment, for learning and memory, for retaining some information, for communication, sending signals to other nearby plants, and even for adaptive decision-making, for growing toward things that are good for them and away from things that are bad for them

Now, this might not mean that plants are sentient, but whether or not it feels like anything to be a plant, they might still be agentic and intelligent in the sense of being able to process some information, being able to adapt to their environment in some ways

I think that can be worth acknowledging.  What would that change about our world and how it functions?  I think that if we seriously considered non-human sentience and welfare, then it would have transformative implications for how we live, but ones that could be very good for humanity as well.  Consider how we relate to food and consider how we relate to wildlife
On the food side, industrial animal agriculture is a leading driver of animal suffering, but then it is also a leading driver of public health and environmental risks for humans

It creates more antibiotic resistance, more disease outbreaks, more extreme weather events via climate change, more biodiversity loss via deforestation.  Similarly, we build an infrastructure primarily for humans, and that can lead to a lot of unnecessary conflict with wildlife

Wildlife can die because they fly into buildings or fly into cars or are trapped in light pollution or trapped in parks with no exit for them if there is a flood or a fire.  If we simply considered their interests when building our infrastructure, then we might be able to build an infrastructure that can be good for human and non-human residents at the same time
But it does require considering human and non-human interests together when making decisions that affect everybody.

title: Did the midterms kill MAGA?
excerpt: Vice President JD Vance gestures as he takes the stage at a campaign rally in Swanton, Ohio, on November 2, 2026. | Tom Brenner/Getty Images In 2015, Donald Tru
body: Vice President JD Vance gestures as he takes the stage at a campaign rally in Swanton, Ohio, on November 2, 2026. | Tom Brenner/Getty Images In 2015, Donald Trump descended a golden escalator and launched a presidential campaign that reshaped American politics

More than a decade later, with his record-low approval ratings and the US embroiled in a war with Iran, he asked voters to treat the 2026 midterms as a referendum on him. “Please pretend I’m on the ballot
Because in a way, I am on the ballot,” Trump told a crowd in North Carolina last month
As it turns out, voters did as Trump asked: Democrats won in a landslide, taking control of both chambers of Congress with victories in Republican strongholds like South Carolina and Kansas

Now, Republicans have to decide what those losses mean for the future of the movement Trump built.  As Vox’s Andrew Prokop reported , there are already competing explanations for the losses that are taking shape on the right. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vice President JD Vance posted on social media
The conservative commentator Erick Erickson offered a longer list of reasons for the GOP’s failure : “It was also the corruption

The overly aggressive deportations.” Others emphasized affordability. “Life is too expensive,” right-wing commentator Benny Johnson wrote . “Especially for young people.” Whoever defines what went wrong will likely help determine which parts of Trump’s politics survive, and who gets to lead the presidential ticket in 2028
The conservative writer Rod Dreher has a stake in that debate
He’s friends with Vance, and he shares the vice president’s interest in combining social conservatism with economic policies that support families
His critiques come from someone who wanted this administration to succeed

Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with Dreher about whether the midterms mean the end of MAGA, what might replace it, and whether Republicans can move past a president who still has two years left in office
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
Before the midterm results even came in, you wrote that Republicans were likely to be shellacked and that they had nobody to blame but Donald Trump and themselves
What do you think it is your fellow conservatives need to admit today?  That MAGA is over
I think there were some good ideas in MAGA and certainly the old Republican establishment, the pre-Trump establishment, needed to go.  But MAGA couldn’t deliver on good government
And if you can’t deliver on good government, it doesn’t matter how charismatic the leader is
And I think that there can be no doubt after this week’s election that it was a complete referendum on Donald Trump and he failed
At the time you wrote that you were aware of some of his failings
I think many people who voted for Trump were aware of some of his failings, but he had a mandate.  He had the popular vote, he had the House, he had the Senate
Why couldn’t MAGA, his movement, deliver on good government?  “But MAGA couldn’t deliver on good government

And if you can’t deliver on good government, it doesn’t matter how charismatic the leader is.” I think that it all comes down to the fact that Trump made decisions based not on rational calculation, by listening to expert advice, but on gut instinct.  I think that the wheels began to fall off of the Trump train on April 2, 2025
That was the so-called Liberation Day when Trump announced these wide tariffs
And that set a pattern for the way that Trump made decisions
Plus. he promoted people not based on competence, but based on loyalty to him, personal loyalty
I think this administration has gone from one crisis to another because of that, because Trump doesn’t have a theory or practice of governance
When he came into office, he signed a bunch of executive orders
Some of them did things that I thought were really good, but he didn’t turn them into legislation

This is a guy whose party held both houses of Congress and the White House, yet he just sailed right along as if he was going to be president forever.  And then of course, this gets us to the Iran war, which was another gut instinct thing by Trump, which became the symbol for all of the disasters of Trumpism
Can MAGA be divorced from Donald Trump? Can it exist without Donald Trump?  No, MAGA is Donald Trump
The challenge is going to be, how does the Republican Party rebuild and regroup for 2028 with Trump still in the White House?  I mean, think about it
They’re fighting a two-front battle now

You’re going to have to fight the Democrats, who are energized, who are going to come in and make the next two years — justifiably, I would say — about investigating Trump administration corruption.  But they’re also going to have to fight Donald Trump himself
Sitting in the White House, he’s not going to shut up
He’s not going to do what is best for his party
He’s going to try to salvage his legacy
What is the next conservative movement? Where do conservatives go from here?  The next few months are going to be really interesting in this respect
Until now, everybody on the right has thought that JD Vance, the vice president, is Trump’s natural successor, even though he hasn’t announced whether or not he’s going to run
I think that has now been called severely into question.  I say this as someone who’s a personal friend of the vice president and would like to see him be president one day

Nevertheless, even though he strongly opposed the Iran war from behind the scenes, he and Marco Rubio and everyone else in this administration are tied to it and all the other failures of Trumpism.  So who does that leave on the outside? title: How Democrats can make good on their new mandate
excerpt: Wes Moore is often mentioned as a potential Democratic presidential candidate in 2028, speculation that he has not exactly batted down. | Monica Morgan/Getty Im
body: Wes Moore is often mentioned as a potential Democratic presidential candidate in 2028, speculation that he has not exactly batted down. | Monica Morgan/Getty Images The midterm elections were great for Democrats everywhere, but some triumphed even more decisively than others: Maryland Gov
Wes Moore, for example, cruised to reelection with roughly 63 percent of the vote

Voters pushed Republicans out — and kept Democrats like Moore in power — in part because of their concerns over a handful of critical issues, including the rising cost of living, the Iran war, and the growing dominance of AI and data centers

The question now is how Democrats can best wield their new power to act on the currents that carried them into office.  For Moore, the stakes may be particularly high: He’s often mentioned as a potential Democratic presidential candidate in 2028, speculation that he has not exactly batted down
America, Actually host Astead Herndon spoke with Moore about his vision for how the Democrats should proceed
As Moore put it, this is a moment in which the party will have to move quickly on the problems that motivate voters most.  Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel
Lowering cost is the top priority for voters, and, frankly, it was where they penalized Trump the most
What’s the single biggest thing Democrats could do to address folks’ cost of living concerns? Actually move fast to fix the things

For example, in Maryland, we’ve done permitting reform to be able to speed up affordable housing, right? And I did not need a 10-year research paper to tell me that we have an issue with affordable housing
If it’s state-owned land, don’t tell me why we can’t do something

The reason we made the largest investments in childcare in our state’s history is because it is insane when you’re watching the fact that people are spending thirty and forty percent of their paychecks on child care and knowing how much that’s actually going to impact [them]
So there are things that we can do right now to be able to address it.  But I also think that there are things that we need Washington to be able to do
For example, gas prices: There’s no governor that can impact gas prices
We just need to stop fighting stupid wars
There’s no governor that is impacting national energy policy or national grocery prices
What we need to do is stop allowing illegal tariff policy to happen
So I do think that there are things that Washington Democrats have got to do, and that they need to move fast on
But I also think that we don’t need to wait for them to be able to put things in place that we know that actually work
I wonder what universal healthcare means to you
Is that the government providing insurance? If you look at what we’ve done here in Maryland, we’ve been able to actually come up with platforms through our Total Cost of Care [Model]
We’re actually working with our hospitals
Our hospitals have a universal budget, and are then able to make sure that people are getting the care that they need
That has done a tremendous job of being able to help to break the cost curve
Maryland is one of the only states in the country where you’re watching the cost of healthcare actually go down, [while] also being able to increase coverage
A lot of the Democrats’ affordability message came out of Mamdani’s win
I remember him telling me the one thing he would never budge on is the belief that billionaires shouldn’t exist
Do you think billionaires should exist? I lose no sleep over the amount of billionaires in our society
I do lose sleep over the amount of children that are growing up in poverty
And I think those who [do] have, have a responsibility to support and uplift and create pathways for those who do not
Here in our state, we actually cut taxes for the middle class

And I said [to wealthy Marylanders], you need to invest more to make sure that we’re doing things like we’re doing: having the fastest public safety turnaround story in the United States of America, having math and reading scores in our public schools now at five-year highs
And I did ask wealthy Marylanders to invest a little bit more to make sure we can get those kinds of results
You served in Afghanistan and are a veteran

When we think about this incoming Democratic Congress, should they continue funding a war that Americans have mostly found is not in their interest? No, and they shouldn’t have funded in the first place.  I’ve heard the argument that that leaves soldiers behind
No, because we’re talking about a president who unilaterally went to war without even asking Congress for authority
The president does not have the authority to just wage war by himself
That is something that the Constitution lays out
Congress is the only one that has the authority for that

And truthfully, this Congress has been so caught up in the aura of the president of the United States that they have not been leaders; they have been cheerleaders.  Part of the issue is that this Congress needs to be held to account, and that’s exactly what I think happened on Tuesday

title: You’re going to hate shopping in an AI economy
excerpt: When was the last time you had to call customer support with a problem? Can you remember how it went?  If you’re like most Americans, the answer is “probab
body: When was the last time you had to call customer support with a problem? Can you remember how it went?  If you’re like most Americans, the answer is “probably not very well.” And that may be understating it: As of 2025, according to the “ National Customer Rage Survey ” — yes, it’s a real thing — nearly 80 percent of Americans ran into a “product or service problem” in the past year, and nearly two-thirds experienced “rage” in attempting to resolve it

We have, in short, entered into a rage economy, where high prices and inflation have made everyday products unaffordable at the same time as our experiences buying those products have filled us with fury

The landscape isn’t really improving, either: As a consumer, you’re faced with terrible customer service, unhelpful chatbots, and products that are worse than they used to be .  If you listen to the big AI companies, however, there’s a light on the horizon: AI agents , which can step in and do the things you don’t want to (like waiting on hold or dueling it out with aforementioned unhelpful chatbots)

But are AI agents really the key to fixing our rage economy? Or will they just be what brings it deeper into chaos? Charlie Warzel , a staff writer at The Atlantic, recently went deep on what happens when we bring AI agents into our already contentious consumer experience (along with his colleague Matteo Wong)

Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with Warzel about how AI agents are being used for the grating parts of our lives, what happens when companies use their own AI agents to deal with consumers, and where this all might leave us.  Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
Charlie, we spoke about how the economy and how customer service works is making everyone rage out
Are AI agents going to make it better or worse? In the early time, it’s probably going to make it a lot worse

What we are essentially seeing right now is that these agents are inundating the internet with persistence.  These are relentless things that are tasked to do the onerous activities that we don’t want to do
And they’re already flooding call centers
They’re flooding restaurant reservations
They’re flooding plumbers and people who run small businesses with requests and queries
And they’re not people.  It’s going to make a lot of people feel, honestly, pretty awful
The world has all of a sudden become very inhuman or there are these inhuman burdens being put on the humans who don’t have agents yet to work on their behalf
And that imbalance is going to make a lot of people pretty mad
You wrote for The Atlantic that we are not ready for our coming AI agent future

How are we not ready for this? If it reaches a critical mass, the argument is that we aren’t ready for it because the economy is built off of, and in a lot of ways thrives off of, inefficiency — off of the fact that people aren’t paying perfect attention to everything.  People aren’t moving their money from savings account to savings account every day because they’re getting the margins on a slightly better interest rate or something like that
This entire subscription economy is based off of inefficiency

You don’t cancel the thing that you don’t use for a long period of time or it lays dormant for a while.  But what these AI agents offer in their most idealized fashion is that they pay perfect attention to everything, all the time
They are hypervigilant and able to act on your behalf in inhuman ways

And if a large portion of the population is using these to do their banking, to do their e-commerce, and at the same time you have these large organizations like banks, healthcare companies, platforms like Amazon and Walmart, you’re going to see just incredible amounts of chaos.  The economy would, in that way, start to behave more like the stock market, where prices fluctuate on the order of milliseconds
And from watching the stock market over decades, I don’t know if we want diapers to behave like securities
One of the more speculative but also illustrative ideas here is what people refer to as an agentic bank run

This is the idea that, say, 5 million people are using the same agent to do all of their banking and they all identify at the same time that there is a high-yield savings account that everyone should be in
So they move money en masse: millions of agents pulling money out of one account to the next, and then those banks are struggling because they’ve just lost all of these deposits at once
It’s theoretically possible that something like that could happen all of the time
Is this a two-way street? Are the companies also adopting agents into every part of their processes and consumer relations? Yes
It’s slower on that end, but I like to think of this as an arms race.  A lot of retailers, especially Amazon, have blocked a number of these agents from accessing their platform

Because even though Amazon can make good money off of these sales, they don’t yet want these companies to have access to their backend infrastructure.  There are a lot of corporate secrets like inventory and who’s buying what and who’s selling what

These agents can act as really good intelligence gatherers if they’re granted access to these platforms.  What you’ll see eventually is that the retailers are going to have demands: “You guys can let the agents on the platform, but you can’t undercut our prices in this way.” It will just be something that you have to trust that your AI agent company is making a deal in your best interest

I think that that’s really interesting because you could end up having this future where everything feels really good as a consumer because it’s frictionless: “My agent’s going to do all this stuff for me while I sleep or while I’m hanging out with my family or whatnot.” And in reality, what’s going to happen is you’re just having someone do something for you, but nothing else has really changed
It’s not that much more helpful to you because these companies have taken care of themselves first

That is what Sam Altman and Mark Zuckerberg are trying to sell us.  Do you think it’s a pipe dream or do you think there is some reality, one day, when we as a society will say, “This consumer-facing AI agent world of ours is better than the one we had a hundred years ago”? Something that I think is really funny is Meta, with Muse, has really dominated the conversation about these AI assistants
And this is the company that wanted to connect the world, that says that us being together is this universal good, it is strengthening the bonds of humanity
This is a tool that is fundamentally antisocial
You don’t have to interact with those people if you don’t want to

I’m not trying to romanticize running really annoying errands when you’re busy and your kids are sick and you’ve got work deadlines and things, but there’s also the experience of interacting with people on a day-to-day basis that is foundational to our humanity and these things basically want to automate that away.  That’s a real thing that we need to think about and grapple with
And the other part of this is, what are we freeing this time up for? I’m always wondering that myself, because that’s what they keep promising
You’re going to have so much time…to do what? To then just spend more time scrolling your platforms? To spend more time scrolling your platforms, spend more time working

There is a lack of thought about what a human is for if we fully embrace automation in all these different ways, right? It’s one thing to say, “I wish it was easier to buy paper towels on Amazon.” It’s another to say— It’s pretty easy, though

title: This election’s biggest AI story isn’t about data centers
excerpt: Abdul El-Sayed, then-Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, speaks during a news conference near the construction site of "The Barn" data center, developed
body: Abdul El-Sayed, then-Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, speaks during a news conference near the construction site of "The Barn" data center, developed by Related Digital for Oracle and OpenAI, in Saline Township, Michigan, on July 30, 2026. | Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images You’ve probably been hearing a lot about data centers this week.  Candidates in several races made regulating data centers a key part of their campaigns
Now, 40 ballot measures to slow or stop data centers have passed

And in an exit poll , when respondents were asked how important AI and data centers were in their vote for Congress, 56 percent answered that it was a “crucial or a major factor.”  Data centers are the physical infrastructure that powers AI, and they’ve become deeply unpopular not just because of their noisiness, ugliness, or electricity demand , but because of what they symbolize: the acceleration of a technology that many Americans fear and that they feel Silicon Valley is foisting upon them.   Key takeaways Key figures to watch include Abdul El-Sayed, Jon Ossoff, and Scott Wiener
Maria Cantwell has already put out a framework that could have bipartisan appeal
Data centers have grabbed the headlines, but the bigger story is the sweeping success of candidates who prioritize AI safety
These leaders will be poised to rein in the tech itself through hearings and lawmaking

If you’re one of the Americans worried about AI — or just prefer a more serious regulatory approach over the hands-off, Trump White House approach — there’s a problem with confining your attention to data centers
Even a successful push against them won’t address the bigger issues around the technology
And picking off data center projects one by one will slow, but not stop, the buildout
AI companies will still find jurisdictions that are willing to let them build — it’ll just cost them more
The election outcome that matters far more, though it was far less trumpeted, is that voters just elected a new crop of leaders promising to actually push to regulate the tech itself
These are people who are concerned not just about AI’s physical infrastructure, but about AI regulation and safety

And they’ve signaled that they’ll push for laws that address the full spectrum of risks from AI — from cyber hacks and job losses all the way to bioweapons, power concentration, and even the possibility of human extinction.  In fact, for AI watchers, one of the most striking things about this election cycle is how safety-pilled many candidates have become since the major AI hacks this summer. “If you go back before the summer, most conversations from policymakers around AI were at a very, very high level of abstraction

Few of them were focused on how these AI models may be highly capable and may pose rather unique risks,” Mackenzie Arnold, an analyst at the Institute for Law & AI, told me. “But there’s been a big shift.”  The midterm results — and the Democrats’ stunning takeover of Congress — improve the odds of reining in AI

But now, the big question is: Can the new victors use the momentum they built up around data centers — the kitchen-table issue that initially brought many voters into the tent — and broaden out beyond that to mobilize for greater AI safety? They may have a lot of ideas, but are they any good? The new (and newly emboldened) crop of AI safety advocates  Among the newly elected Democrats, a striking number are very vocal about AI risks
And a few have clearly taken the time to educate themselves on the finer points

So before considering what concrete changes they can actually implement, it’s worth getting to know what they’ve proposed.  Abdul El-Sayed , who won the Michigan Senate race, said that we need a “full-on pause” on frontier AI research
He’s also advocated for global coordination on a slowdown, including a treaty with China aimed at avoiding an arms race dynamic
He supports a ban on recursive self-improvement, where AI models build the next, even smarter AI models
He also wants a new federal safety agency that would inspect companies and block releases if necessary

Even if not all his ideas resonate with experts (like the simplistic idea of a “kill switch” for dangerous models), having him in the Senate means that AI safety advocates will have an easier time arguing for a pause on frontier research.  Another winner to watch is Jon Ossoff , who prevailed in his Georgia Senate race

In his victory speech, he lambasted AI developers, saying, “The titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.”  Back in September, he impressed safety advocates by explicitly mentioning “catastrophic risks” like AI-engineered bioweapons

Conveying his priorities, he said , “A capable president would move swiftly to secure and reassure the American people, rush inspectors into frontier labs, fortify the nation against bioterrorism, demand legislation from Congress, and lead the world toward an AI treaty
But President Trump is compromised.”  Two other Democrats with strong AI safety bona fides and specific policy ideas have emerged victorious this week

Scott Wiener — the longtime California state senator who was behind two important pieces of legislation, SB 1047 (which was ultimately vetoed ) and SB 53 (which was signed into law) — won Nancy Pelosi’s seat this week

He’s said he’ll work to institute strict federal safety standards and “guard against catastrophic risk from AI.”  And Manny Rutinel — who cosponsored a 2024 law that sought to regulate AI use — won his race in Colorado

Rutinel has ties to effective altruism, a movement long preoccupied with AI safety, and you can hear it in the way he talks: “This technology has a 10 percent risk of wiping out human civilization,” he recently told The New York Times. “I don’t want human civilization to come to an end.” Sam Forstag, who just became Montana’s first Democratic member of Congress in decades, also stated that AI poses an “existential risk to all of humanity.” Troy Jackson, the Democrat who won his Senate race in Maine, has vowed that he’s “not going to let the billionaires write the rules,” adding , “We are not that far from ‘Terminator,’ and I don’t want to be ‘hasta la vista, baby.’”  You can expect these new victors to be reliable votes supporting the cause of AI regulation come early 2027

But what, exactly, might that look like? What Democrats plan to do now on AI As Democrats are poised to take power in Congress, they will have two big levers to pull on AI safety: hearings and lawmaking.  Now that the election is over, expect a whole lot of hearings

Ed Markey, who won reelection in Massachusetts, signaled that he’s coming for Big Tech executives. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” he posted on X

What will it look like if these executives are called to testify under oath? “Some of the hearings are going to be focused on safety practices — and evidence that the company’s practices are not up to snuff,” Arnold told me. “Asking for answers to questions of:  ‘Why didn’t you find that earlier? Why didn’t you tell us?’ And while that doesn’t get you all the way [to safety], this public pressure is why so many companies have adopted voluntary practices, why they’ve improved their internal monitoring, their incident reporting, their response time to various incidents.” As for lawmaking, experts I spoke with are now bullish that we’ll see much stronger AI legislation in 2027 than we’ve seen to date
Maria Cantwell, who’s slated to chair the Senate Commerce Committee, is a key player to watch
She’s already put out a framework for governing AI that could have bipartisan appeal, which she’s called a precursor to legislation

It requires mandatory safety standards for cutting-edge AI models, independent testing and audits that models would have to pass before release, and prompt reporting of safety incidents. “Cantwell is going to push that, and she’s in a place to basically be the voice of the caucus on that,” Brad Carson, an advocate for stricter AI policies who leads Americans for Responsible AI and a former congressman, told me. “Every single Democrat supports it, and all they need is five or six Republicans to beat the filibuster, and I bet you they can find that.” Carson is hopeful that Democrats can get Republican votes “especially as the gravitational pull of the White House eases,” he said. “Trump has led them down the primrose path of defeat
A lot of smart politicians are going to be distancing themselves.” Yes, President Donald Trump ultimately holds veto power
And he’s allowed American tech companies to race ahead on the technology with very few guardrails

But as AI companies make more and more concessions to safety in light of security incidents, the president may be more willing to sign on to some safety regulations.  “He’s mercurial enough that I can see him signing something like this,” Carson told me, “especially if some of these Republicans say, ‘Look, we’re getting battered on data centers and AI
Let’s do this.’” Of course, the most surefire way to gain control of AI lawmaking, unobstructed by a veto, would be to lay the groundwork for a Democratic White House in 2028

And the midterms showed that a focus on reining in AI can help propel Democrats to victory. “The road to 2028 starts today,” wrote Alex Bores , the New York Assembly member who has made AI his main focus. “In order to maintain voters’ trust and avoid catastrophic risk, we need a unified baseline around AI safety in the Democratic Party.” Although many voters focused on data centers this election cycle, it’s reasonable to predict — as cyber breaches and other security incidents proliferate — that they will move from symbol to substance, focusing more on safety in the run-up to 2028.    “We shouldn’t view voter sentiment towards data centers and AI as stagnant or static,” Arnold told me. “I think it will continue to update to events in the world, and I think it will increasingly focus on AI itself as we see events in the world that make that very obvious to people.” Or as Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus that sets policy and legislative strategy, put it , “The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election, and in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics.” The savviest politicians are already preparing with that earthquake in mind.

title: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
excerpt: A robot cleaned my apartment for $30 — San Francisco startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots into people's homes, piloted remotely by humans who co
body: A robot cleaned my apartment for $30 — San Francisco startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots into people's homes, piloted remotely by humans who collect training data while the robots clean — making the service cheaper than you'd expect for something this futuristic
Cute but clumsy — The four-and-a-half-foot robot climbed stairs like it was drunk, knocked over olive oil, and left taps dripping — but impressively reattached its toilet brush wand three times

The Jetsons, with caveats — If autonomous cleaning robots become real, the human cost could be steep: cleaning workers could lose their jobs, and U.S. policy is nowhere near ready to handle that. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148090" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner
I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser
But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist
I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour
I was also motivated by journalistic interest
In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up

Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists
As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants
Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round
Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product
At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit
But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain

They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.  But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute

Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks)
Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors
With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos

Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them
These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data
Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there

But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help

If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide
The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle
It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee
That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door
I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps
Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing

When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said
Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps

As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment

Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.) You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though
Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist

I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger
In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet

That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle
The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta
It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled
But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was
As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out

title: Pope Leo’s trip is a homecoming to Peru – where debate over liberation theology roiled the church during his early years as a priest

<title>Pope Leo’s trip is a homecoming to Peru – where debate over liberation theology roiled the church during his early years as a priest</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770403/original/file-20261105-64-909jxl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7102%2C4734&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A mototaxi drives past a banner of Pope Leo XIV in Chiclayo, Peru, on Nov. 5, 2026, ahead of his trip to Latin America.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/PeruPope/7296c0075d304da7a2ef4351555684f7/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=pope%20leo&amp;currentItemNo=2&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Martin Mejia</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Pope Leo XIV travels to Latin America on Nov. 6, 2026, with <a href="https://press.vatican.va/content/salastampa/it/bollettino/pubblico/2026/09/21/0736/01738.html#en">a packed itinerary</a> that will bring him through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It is Leo’s first trip to the region since his elevation to the papacy – and a homecoming for <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-pope-is-peruvian-how-2-decades-in-south-america-shaped-the-vision-of-pope-leo-xiv-256415">a pope who spent two decades in Peru</a> and holds Peruvian citizenship.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://www.rit.edu/directory/eblgla-eben-levey">a historian</a> of <a href="https://doi.org/10.13016/4bla-77sh">Catholicism in the late 20th century</a>, I couldn’t help but notice that <a href="https://press.vatican.va/content/salastampa/it/bollettino/pubblico/2026/09/21/0736/01738.html">the pope’s plans</a> walk a fine line during a fraught political moment in Latin America.</p>

<p>Leo plans to meet with the <a href="https://en.mercopress.com/2026/11/03/the-pope-arrives-in-an-argentina-where-bishops-are-among-milei-s-firmest-critics">right-wing presidents of Argentina</a> <a href="https://www.ncronline.org/vatican/vatican-news/pope-leos-latin-america-trip-high-stakes-homecoming">and Peru</a>. He will also visit sites often associated with the progressive wing of the Catholic Church, including Casavalle, one of the <a href="https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20261101-seen-and-heard-uruguay-neighborhood-places-hopes-in-pope">poorest neighborhoods</a> in Uruguay’s capital. In Argentina, where President Javier Milei has <a href="https://apnews.com/article/argentina-javier-milei-trump-disabilities-austerity-6d98fb3cecc91fe4f3e3f8800826275e">drastically cut</a> funding for disability services, the pope will go to a Catholic home for disabled people.</p>

<p>And in Chiclayo, Peru, where Leo served as a bishop, he will pray at a chapel dedicated to St. Óscar Romero. A Salvadoran archbishop, Romero <a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/assassination-of-a-saint/paper">was assassinated in 1980</a> after years of speaking out against the human rights violations committed by the <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/36700/the-massacre-at-el-mozote-by-mark-danner/">U.S.-supported</a> <a href="https://www.calmigration.org/learn-chapter/civil-war">Salvadoran military</a>. His ministry was influenced by <a href="https://theconversation.com/after-50-years-liberation-theology-is-still-reshaping-catholicism-and-politics-but-what-is-it-186804">liberation theology</a>, a controversial movement born in Peru that roiled church politics for decades – including during Leo’s years in Peru.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770404/original/file-20261105-64-hzvkma.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A close-up photo of someone's two cupped hands, holding a gold and silver ornament with a picture of a priest with glasses." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770404/original/file-20261105-64-hzvkma.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770404/original/file-20261105-64-hzvkma.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770404/original/file-20261105-64-hzvkma.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770404/original/file-20261105-64-hzvkma.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770404/original/file-20261105-64-hzvkma.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770404/original/file-20261105-64-hzvkma.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770404/original/file-20261105-64-hzvkma.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
