            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What is liberation theology?</h2>

<p>The name itself was coined in a 1968 lecture by <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/23/world/americas/gustavo-gutierrez-dead.html">Gustavo Gutiérrez</a>, a Peruvian theologian and priest. He expanded on his ideas in a 1971 book, “<a href="https://orbisbooks.com/products/9781626985414?srsltid=AYCX9vIJkIEBTafm65WkZiA2WWXGZFkSkEwMIPHf0HdvB5Xz2kRYparw">A Theology of Liberation</a>.” </p>

<p>Gutiérrez and like-minded theologians argued that Christians have a moral duty <a href="https://theconversation.com/after-50-years-liberation-theology-is-still-reshaping-catholicism-and-politics-but-what-is-it-186804">to liberate the oppressed</a>. They saw poverty, violence, racism and discrimination as not just problems but collective sins. While building on earlier Catholic social teachings, these “liberationists” envisioned profound change that went beyond the spiritual care and charitable work of traditional Latin American Catholicism. </p>

<p>Catholics <a href="https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/E/bo3631145.html">inspired by liberation theology</a> created community organizations and work cooperatives, organized labor unions and fostered other initiatives that sought to measurably improve the lives of the poor. In <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/liberation-theology-and-the-others-9781793633637/">my own research</a>, I’ve documented how priests and nuns in rural Mexico helped organize transportation, corn milling and carpentry cooperatives.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770405/original/file-20261105-64-4e1iix.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A black and white photo of a man in a sweater, collarded shirt and glasses holding up his finger as he speaks." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770405/original/file-20261105-64-4e1iix.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770405/original/file-20261105-64-4e1iix.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=863&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770405/original/file-20261105-64-4e1iix.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=863&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770405/original/file-20261105-64-4e1iix.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=863&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770405/original/file-20261105-64-4e1iix.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1084&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770405/original/file-20261105-64-4e1iix.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1084&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770405/original/file-20261105-64-4e1iix.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1084&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Gustavo Gutiérrez’s writings provided the foundation for liberation theology in the 1960s and ’70s.</span>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Gutiérrez also argued that Christians should use Marxist ideas about <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/pedagogy-of-the-oppressed-9781501314131/">analyzing society and the economy</a> to <a href="https://monthlyreview.org/9780853450931/">better understand inequality</a>. In nations like Peru, <a href="https://doi.org/10.4324/9780429315060">which possessed rich natural resources</a>, liberationists tailored their economic justice projects to address how international and national companies profited off the low wages of miners and farmers.</p>

<p>During the Cold War, however, these ideas led some politicians and church leaders to accuse liberationists of socialism and communism.</p>

<p>A minority fringe of liberationists did embrace left-ring radicalism. <a href="https://kellogg.nd.edu/space-utopia-christians-socialism-chile">Christians for Socialism</a>, for example, argued that liberation <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/blog/2025/12/12/the-chilean-christians-for-socialism-movement-liberationist-third-worldist-and-utopian/">meant rejecting capitalism</a>. Some clergy, although only a handful, even <a href="https://www.routledge.com/Camilo-Torres-Priest-Liberation-Theologian-Guerrilla-Fighter/Ginzberg/p/book/9781032990255">picked up arms</a> to fight alongside clandestine left-wing revolutionary groups. </p>

<h2>A wary pope</h2>

<p>This presented a dilemma to the Vatican. </p>

<p>In 1891, Pope Leo XIII – <a href="https://theconversation.com/19th-century-catholic-teachings-21st-century-tech-how-concerns-about-ai-guided-pope-leos-choice-of-name-256645">the current pope’s namesake</a> – <a href="https://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiii/en/encyclicals/documents/hf_l-xiii_enc_15051891_rerum-novarum.html">published “Rerum Novarum</a>,” an encyclical focused on workers’ rights amid the Industrial Revolution. Since then, the Vatican had critiqued the worst excesses of capitalism while also rejecting socialism and communism, which it viewed as godless ideologies. </p>

<p>During the 1960s and ’70s, Pope Paul VI generally <a href="https://www.commonwealmagazine.org/introduction-%E2%80%98commonweal%E2%80%99-and-liberation-theology">supported local initiatives by liberationist Catholics</a>, including some <a href="https://www.nybooks.com/online/2026/05/24/the-education-of-pope-leo-xiv/">in Chulucanas, Peru</a>, where Leo began his missionary work. Paul appointed and elevated bishops who shared a vision that the church could help empower the poor and alleviate oppression. </p>

<p>But the Vatican shifted when the Polish cardinal Karol Józef Wojtyla became Pope John Paul II in 1978. For most of his adult life, Poland had been part of the Soviet bloc, which imposed restrictions on organized religion. A <a href="https://www.anneapplebaum.com/2005/04/06/how-the-pope-defeated-communism/">staunch opponent of communism</a>, <a href="https://time.com/archive/6854086/religion-john-paul-vs-liberation-theology/">he worried about liberation theology’s</a> use of Marxist analysis. So did one of his top Vatican officials, Joseph Ratzinger – the future Pope Benedict XVI.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770406/original/file-20261105-64-ei7hcy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man in white vestments kneels in the grass in front of a slab of stone while a crowd of people look on." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770406/original/file-20261105-64-ei7hcy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770406/original/file-20261105-64-ei7hcy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770406/original/file-20261105-64-ei7hcy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770406/original/file-20261105-64-ei7hcy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770406/original/file-20261105-64-ei7hcy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770406/original/file-20261105-64-ei7hcy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770406/original/file-20261105-64-ei7hcy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Pope John Paul II prays at the tomb of anti-communist dissident priest Jerzy Popieluszko, in front of the Church of St. Stanislas in Warsaw, on June 14, 1987.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/pope-john-paul-ii-prays-14-june-1987-in-warsaw-in-front-of-news-photo/136742376?phrase=%22john%20paul%22%20communism&amp;adppopup=true">Jean-Claude Delmas/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The Vatican began investigating <a href="https://wipfandstock.com/products/marx-and-the-bible-9781592444854?srsltid=AYCX9vK51gjTntA4LFREX5-quPazIhRZj3zxLHw_WdGvf0hAHqxu3p6B">some liberation theologians</a> for violations of church teachings. In 1985, for example, Brazilian liberationist theologian Leonardo Boff was ordered to observe a <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/813628776">year of silence</a> – no publishing, no public speaking – to discipline him for his critique of the church’s hierarchy. Several priests <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-28656661">were suspended</a> <a href="https://www.americamagazine.org/news/2016/02/23/nicaragua-jesuit-fernando-cardenal-dies-82/">over their work</a> in Sandinista Nicaragua.</p>

<p>John Paul ordered that the Peruvian bishops begin an investigation of Gutiérrez – above all, over <a href="https://www.ncronline.org/news/theology/vatican-doctrinal-czar-liberation-theology-pioneer-reflects-troubles">Marxism’s influence on his work</a>. Gutiérrez was ultimately not punished. </p>

<p>One factor in his favor may have been his consistent opposition to armed revolution, even before violence raged in Peru from the 1980s into the ’90s. <a href="https://www.dukeupress.edu/Shining-and-Other-Paths">The Shining Path</a>, a Maoist guerrilla group, was waging a war of terrorism against the Peruvian government, setting off bombs across Peru. </p>

<p>Under President Alberto Fujimori, the government escalated existing counterinsurgency operations, often using indiscriminate violence against citizens in the region where the Shining Path emerged. In 2009, Fujimori was convicted of <a href="https://academic.oup.com/ijtj/article-abstract/3/3/384/2888395?redirectedFrom=fulltext">human rights violations</a>.</p>

<h2>Young priest</h2>

<p>Leo has never described himself as a liberationist Catholic. However, his experiences as a priest were <a href="https://www.nybooks.com/online/2026/05/24/the-education-of-pope-leo-xiv/">indelibly shaped by liberation theology</a>, the Peruvian armed conflict and the church debates that roiled much of Latin America during his years there.</p>

<p>Leo, born Robert Prevost, was raised in Chicago. After ordination, his journey as a priest began in Peru, where he landed for missionary work in 1985. The young friar followed in the footsteps of other <a href="https://undpress.nd.edu/9780268029050/maryknoll-catholic-mission-in-peru-1943-1989/">U.S. Catholic missionaries</a> who had been serving among Peru’s poor and Indigenous, urban and rural, since the 1940s.</p>

<figure class="align-left zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770408/original/file-20261105-64-8u2bf4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A black and white portrait of a man with dark hair in a suit and tie." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770408/original/file-20261105-64-8u2bf4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770408/original/file-20261105-64-8u2bf4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=790&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770408/original/file-20261105-64-8u2bf4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=790&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770408/original/file-20261105-64-8u2bf4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=790&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770408/original/file-20261105-64-8u2bf4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=993&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770408/original/file-20261105-64-8u2bf4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=993&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770408/original/file-20261105-64-8u2bf4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=993&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Photo_of_Robert_Prevost_in_Villanova_yearbook_1977.jpg">Nova Nationer/Facebook via Wikimedia Commons</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Sent to Chulucanas, in Peru’s coastal northwest, Prevost found himself in a region of pastoral experimentation. Since the 1960s, Augustinian missionaries had been <a href="https://www.nybooks.com/online/2026/05/24/the-education-of-pope-leo-xiv/">working closely</a> with the community to provide literacy education, discussion groups about poverty and inequality, and workshops to train artisans. </p>

<p>These programs were a far cry from the more radical actions of some Catholics who supported liberation theology. Nevertheless, the programs in Chulucanas aimed to empower the Peruvian poor, chipping away at exploitation and low wages on the region’s sugarcane and cotton estates. Like Gutiérrez, many Peruvian Christians believed that the Shining Path <a href="https://doi.org/10.1179/1462317X13Z.0000000004">drew support because of pervasive poverty and inequality</a>, and that churches could help transform the nation. </p>

<p>But the Catholic Church in Latin America was in the midst of another transformation. John Paul gradually appointed <a href="https://www.routledge.com/The-Politics-of-Transnational-Actors-in-Latin-America-Power-from-Afar/Shepherd/p/book/9781138096332">conservative bishops</a> across the continent. Experimental pastoral programs lost support, and institutions that trained priests to put liberation theology into action, such as the <a href="https://doi.org/10.13016/4bla-77sh">Regional Seminary of the Southeast</a> in Mexico, were shuttered or “reoriented.” </p>

<p>Yet even as the hierarchy shifted conservative, work on the ground among Latin America’s poorest continued apace. From <a href="https://press.umich.edu/Books/D/Divined-Intervention2">coffee cooperatives in Mexico</a> to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1515/9783111726069">human rights activists</a> across the continent, many programs survived.</p>

<h2>‘Cease the repression’</h2>

<p>Leo’s 2026 itinerary includes multiple stops that speak to this history and on-the-ground pastoral work. The most symbolic, perhaps, is the Capilla San Óscar Romero, located in Chiclayo, the pope’s former diocese.</p>

<p>A neighborhood chapel <a href="https://www.latintimes.com/pope-leo-xiv-visit-chiclayo-chapel-600527">renovated with donations</a> from Leo’s connections in the United States, it is one of many sites throughout the Americas honoring Catholics who fell victim to right-wing, anti-communist violence. The day before Romero’s assassination, he used his weekly radio address to speak directly to El Salvador’s conscripted soldiers, telling them, “<a href="https://sojo.net/magazine/may-1980/pastors-last-homily">No soldier is obliged to obey an order counter to the law of God</a>.”</p>

<p>Leo XIV’s visit to the chapel is for private prayer, not a homily or a speech. Still, I would argue that the soft-spoken pope’s stop will evoke Romero’s message – especially at a time of <a href="https://apnews.com/article/rubio-peru-drug-trafficking-trump-b625fe79a901799707343ff5dd83b5f4">strikes against suspected drug traffickers</a>, which <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2025/09/18/us-maritime-strikes-amount-to-extrajudicial-killings">human rights groups</a> have <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/ck5ye7v88qy7o">criticized as extrajudicial killings</a>. <a href="https://sojo.net/magazine/may-1980/pastors-last-homily">During his final Mass</a>, Romero pleaded, “I beseech you, I beg you, I command you in the name of God: Cease the repression!”</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294299/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

AP Photo/Martin Mejia Pope Leo XIV travels to Latin America on Nov. 6, 2026, with a packed itinerary that will bring him through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru
It is Leo’s first trip to the region since his elevation to the papacy – and a homecoming for a pope who spent two decades in Peru and holds Peruvian citizenship
As a historian of Catholicism in the late 20th century , I couldn’t help but notice that the pope’s plans walk a fine line during a fraught political moment in Latin America
Leo plans to meet with the right-wing presidents of Argentina and Peru
He will also visit sites often associated with the progressive wing of the Catholic Church, including Casavalle, one of the poorest neighborhoods in Uruguay’s capital
In Argentina, where President Javier Milei has drastically cut funding for disability services, the pope will go to a Catholic home for disabled people
And in Chiclayo, Peru, where Leo served as a bishop, he will pray at a chapel dedicated to St. Óscar Romero
A Salvadoran archbishop, Romero was assassinated in 1980 after years of speaking out against the human rights violations committed by the U.S.-supported Salvadoran military
His ministry was influenced by liberation theology , a controversial movement born in Peru that roiled church politics for decades – including during Leo’s years in Peru
Oscar Romero during a religious procession honoring him in San Salvador, El Salvador, on Aug. 1, 2024
AP Photo/Salvador Melendez What is liberation theology? The name itself was coined in a 1968 lecture by Gustavo Gutiérrez , a Peruvian theologian and priest
He expanded on his ideas in a 1971 book, “ A Theology of Liberation .” Gutiérrez and like-minded theologians argued that Christians have a moral duty to liberate the oppressed
They saw poverty, violence, racism and discrimination as not just problems but collective sins

While building on earlier Catholic social teachings, these “liberationists” envisioned profound change that went beyond the spiritual care and charitable work of traditional Latin American Catholicism

Catholics inspired by liberation theology created community organizations and work cooperatives, organized labor unions and fostered other initiatives that sought to measurably improve the lives of the poor
In my own research , I’ve documented how priests and nuns in rural Mexico helped organize transportation, corn milling and carpentry cooperatives
Gustavo Gutiérrez’s writings provided the foundation for liberation theology in the 1960s and ’70s
Bettmann/Getty Images Gutiérrez also argued that Christians should use Marxist ideas about analyzing society and the economy to better understand inequality

In nations like Peru, which possessed rich natural resources , liberationists tailored their economic justice projects to address how international and national companies profited off the low wages of miners and farmers
During the Cold War, however, these ideas led some politicians and church leaders to accuse liberationists of socialism and communism
A minority fringe of liberationists did embrace left-ring radicalism
Christians for Socialism , for example, argued that liberation meant rejecting capitalism
Some clergy, although only a handful, even picked up arms to fight alongside clandestine left-wing revolutionary groups
A wary pope This presented a dilemma to the Vatican
In 1891, Pope Leo XIII – the current pope’s namesake – published “Rerum Novarum ,” an encyclical focused on workers’ rights amid the Industrial Revolution
Since then, the Vatican had critiqued the worst excesses of capitalism while also rejecting socialism and communism, which it viewed as godless ideologies
During the 1960s and ’70s, Pope Paul VI generally supported local initiatives by liberationist Catholics , including some in Chulucanas, Peru , where Leo began his missionary work
Paul appointed and elevated bishops who shared a vision that the church could help empower the poor and alleviate oppression
But the Vatican shifted when the Polish cardinal Karol Józef Wojtyla became Pope John Paul II in 1978
For most of his adult life, Poland had been part of the Soviet bloc, which imposed restrictions on organized religion
A staunch opponent of communism , he worried about liberation theology’s use of Marxist analysis
So did one of his top Vatican officials, Joseph Ratzinger – the future Pope Benedict XVI

<title>Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms stands on the shoulders of Stacey Abrams, Charlotta Bass and countless other Black women who dreamed</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770533/original/file-20261106-64-2n6ykk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3824%2C2549&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms hugs her daughter Lincoln during an election night watch party in Atlanta, Ga., on Nov. 3, 2026. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/georgia-gov-elect-keisha-lance-bottoms-hugs-her-daughter-news-photo/2303419319?phrase=keisha%20lance%20bottoms%20daughter&amp;adppopup=true">Megan Varner/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>There are elections that change the political map. And then there are elections that make you wonder whether the land itself remembers.</p>

<p>Georgia remembers.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/horrors-great-slave-auction-180962287/">The auction blocks</a>. <a href="https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/slavery-in-antebellum-georgia/">The cotton fields</a>. <a href="https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/lynching/">The lynching trees</a>. The Black women who cleaned governors’ homes but could not dream of becoming governor themselves.</p>

<p>And now Keisha Lance Bottoms has been elected <a href="https://apnews.com/article/georgia-governor-lance-bottom-jackson-midterm-election-67c22a38b9a6e4cad5584aa44acf106f">Georgia’s first Black woman governor</a>. The first Black woman elected governor of any American state.</p>

<p>Bottoms has <a href="https://www.ajc.com/politics/2026/11/keisha-lance-bottoms-crawfordville-governors-mansion/">traced her ancestry back five generations</a> to an enslaved person on a plantation near Crawfordville, Georgia. </p>

<p>An ancestor held in bondage on Georgia soil. A descendant elected to govern it.</p>

<p>The same earth. An entirely different claim to power. How many women had to believe in a future they would never live to see?</p>

<p>Bottoms’s victory represents the paradox of Black political advancement amid racial violence and the often-unrecognized labor of women who build futures they may never inhabit. Ultimately, Bottoms’ victory reflects both extraordinary progress and the unfinished work of American democracy. </p>



<h2>The children who deserved a future</h2>

<p>I keep thinking about the little children.</p>

<p>Between 1979 and 1981, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2019/04/30/us/atlanta-child-murders.html">Atlanta was terrorized</a> by the disappearances and murders of Black children and young adults. Mothers pleaded for answers. Families lived in a city where childhood itself had become dangerous.</p>

<p>The murders unfolded just years after <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1973/10/17/archives/atlanta-elects-a-black-mayor-first-in-a-major-southern-city-black.html">Maynard Jackson’s historic 1973 election</a> as Atlanta’s first Black mayor. His victory announced a new era of Black political power. Yet that power could not shield the city’s most vulnerable children. <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/2005/08/07/klan-was-probed-in-child-killings-in-atlanta/334ee8d7-5322-428a-9ebe-d05efaacf19b/">Suspicions of Ku Klux Klan involvement circulated</a>, although the Klan’s responsibility was never established.</p>

<p>That distinction matters. So does the fear.</p>

<p><a href="https://blackpast.org/african-american-history/keisha-lance-bottoms-1970/">Bottoms was born in 1970</a>. She was 9 when the murders began. She grew up in the same Atlanta where Black parents searched desperately for their missing children. She belonged to the generation whose futures were being stolen. And now she is preparing to lead the entire state.</p>

<p>What a terrible, beautiful, complicated thing.</p>

<p>Those murdered children were not symbols waiting to become useful to history. They were sons and daughters who deserved the ordinary miracle of growing older. They deserved a future. </p>

<p><a href="https://nul.org/basic-page/state-black-america-mayor-keisha-lance-bottoms">Bottoms later occupied the mayor’s office</a> that Jackson first opened to Black leadership. Now she is preparing to occupy the governor’s mansion. History has not erased its cruelty. But it has delivered an astonishing answer. </p>

<p>And this victory does not belong to Bottoms alone.</p>

<h2>The woman who sowed the seeds</h2>

<p>This victory belongs, in no small measure, to <a href="https://civilrightsmuseum.org/blog/stacey-abrams-champion-of-voting-rights-honored-at-the-national-civil-rights-museum/">democracy advocate, legislator and lawyer Stacey Abrams</a>. Perhaps those who recognize what Abrams made possible have sent her flowers. </p>

<p>Abrams ran for Georgia governor in 2018 and 2022. She <a href="https://atlanta.capitalbnews.org/abrams-loss-recap/">lost both races</a>. But through the <a href="https://slsvcoalition.org/partner/new-georgia-project/">New Georgia Project</a> and <a href="https://fairfight.com/">Fair Fight</a>, organizations focused on engaging voters and protecting voting rights, she helped build an electorate that could imagine Georgia differently. <a href="https://www.britannica.com/question/How-has-Stacey-Abrams-worked-to-protect-voting-rights">She registered voters, challenged barriers to participation</a>, and refused to accept that the South’s political future was fixed.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770531/original/file-20261106-64-v5o966.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A crowd of people holding signs and paying attention to someone not in the photo." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770531/original/file-20261106-64-v5o966.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770531/original/file-20261106-64-v5o966.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770531/original/file-20261106-64-v5o966.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770531/original/file-20261106-64-v5o966.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770531/original/file-20261106-64-v5o966.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770531/original/file-20261106-64-v5o966.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770531/original/file-20261106-64-v5o966.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Supporters listen as Democratic gubernatorial candidate Stacey Abrams speaks at a rally in Atlanta, Ga., on Nov. 5, 2022.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/democratic-supporters-listen-as-democratic-gubernatorial-news-photo/1244566907?phrase=stacey%20abrams%20crowd&amp;adppopup=true">Nathan Posner/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>And now another Black woman has won the office Abrams twice sought, in the third gubernatorial race in a row <a href="https://amsterdamnews.com/news/2026/11/03/keisha-lance-bottoms-wins-georgia-governor/">headed by a Black Democratic woman</a>. There is something biblical about the path Abrams steadfastly cleared. I think of Moses, guiding his people toward the Promised Land but never entering it himself. </p>

<p>Abrams’ journey is not over. Nor should her accomplishments be measured by another woman’s victory. But I believe there is sacred work in preparing a future you may never personally enjoy. Some people plant trees. Some people sit in their shade. Stacey Abrams planted. Bottoms is standing beneath the branches.</p>

<p>And as <a href="https://annenberg.usc.edu/faculty/allissa-v-richardson">a scholar of Black media history</a>, I can reach even further back, to another woman who understood the audacity of claiming political power: <a href="https://scetv.pbslearningmedia.org/resource/ull20-charlotta-spears-bass-video/unladylike2020/">Charlotta Bass</a>. </p>

<p>In 1952, Bass became <a href="https://www.womenshistory.org/education-resources/biographies/charlotta-spears-bass">the first Black woman nominated for vice president</a> of the United States, running on the Progressive Party ticket. </p>

<h2>The future Charlotta dared to imagine</h2>

<p>Before the <a href="https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/voting-rights-act">Voting Rights Act</a> in 1965, before <a href="https://naacp.org/find-resources/history-explained/1963-march-washington">the March on Washington</a> in 1963, before <a href="https://www.nps.gov/features/malu/feat0002/wof/Maynard_Jackson.htm">Jackson was elected mayor</a> in 1973 and before Abrams or Bottoms drew their first breaths, there was Bass. </p>

<p>A Black newspaper publisher who <a href="https://pdf.core.ac.uk/corefilesystem/pdf/3479/232565552.pdf?se=2026-11-06T14%3A49%3A25Z&amp;sp=r&amp;sv=2026-10-06&amp;sr=b&amp;rscd=inline%3B%20filename%3D%22232565552.pdf%22&amp;rsct=application/pdf&amp;sig=Y7M28jTj/2PaKi3HGTqRECrtsAL1wcvmVpZVSCC87xI%3D">confronted segregation, police brutality and white supremacist violence</a> in her four-decade ownership of <a href="https://www.pbs.org/blackpress/news_bios/ca_eagle.html">The California Eagle</a>, Bass understood that political power was about more than winning office. It was about who had the right to imagine themselves in one.</p>



<p>Bass ran when <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2020/08/14/us/charlotta-bass-kamala-harris-trnd">a Black woman entering the White House</a> seemed almost unimaginable. Almost. But not to her. I imagine she would have loved this election. And I suspect she would have had pointed questions for Gov.-elect Bottoms.</p>

<p>What will you do for the poor? The disenfranchised? How will you protect the vote that brought you here? </p>

<p>History-making is not the same as justice-making, and representation matters. The true measure of Bottoms’ victory will be whether Georgians experience the more just state <a href="https://www.wrdw.com/2026/11/03/billionaire-rick-jackson-atlanta-ex-mayor-keisha-lance-bottoms-vie-lead-georgia/">she promised to bring about</a>.</p>

<h2>The work beyond the win</h2>

<p>For generations, <a href="https://www.basicbooks.com/titles/martha-s-jones/vanguard/9781541618619/">Black women have been asked to save a democracy</a> that would not save them. We have carried clipboards, protest signs and entire movements on our backs. We have been told to wait. To be patient. To be grateful.</p>

<p>And now a Black woman has been elected to govern Georgia. </p>

<p>The children have not returned. The past has not been undone. But something has shifted. Charlotta dreamed it. Stacey helped build it. Keisha has won it. And somewhere, another little Black girl is watching. She may not understand the history. She may only know that the governor-elect looks like her. For now, that is enough to begin a dream.</p>

<p>And history has taught us what can happen when a Black girl begins to dream.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296027/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Megan Varner/Getty Images There are elections that change the political map
And then there are elections that make you wonder whether the land itself remembers
The Black women who cleaned governors’ homes but could not dream of becoming governor themselves
And now Keisha Lance Bottoms has been elected Georgia’s first Black woman governor
The first Black woman elected governor of any American state
Bottoms has traced her ancestry back five generations to an enslaved person on a plantation near Crawfordville, Georgia
An ancestor held in bondage on Georgia soil

How many women had to believe in a future they would never live to see? Bottoms’s victory represents the paradox of Black political advancement amid racial violence and the often-unrecognized labor of women who build futures they may never inhabit
Ultimately, Bottoms’ victory reflects both extraordinary progress and the unfinished work of American democracy
The children who deserved a future I keep thinking about the little children
Between 1979 and 1981, Atlanta was terrorized by the disappearances and murders of Black children and young adults
Families lived in a city where childhood itself had become dangerous
The murders unfolded just years after Maynard Jackson’s historic 1973 election as Atlanta’s first Black mayor
His victory announced a new era of Black political power
Yet that power could not shield the city’s most vulnerable children
Suspicions of Ku Klux Klan involvement circulated , although the Klan’s responsibility was never established
She grew up in the same Atlanta where Black parents searched desperately for their missing children
She belonged to the generation whose futures were being stolen
And now she is preparing to lead the entire state
What a terrible, beautiful, complicated thing
Those murdered children were not symbols waiting to become useful to history
They were sons and daughters who deserved the ordinary miracle of growing older
Bottoms later occupied the mayor’s office that Jackson first opened to Black leadership
Now she is preparing to occupy the governor’s mansion
But it has delivered an astonishing answer
And this victory does not belong to Bottoms alone
The woman who sowed the seeds This victory belongs, in no small measure, to democracy advocate, legislator and lawyer Stacey Abrams
Perhaps those who recognize what Abrams made possible have sent her flowers
Abrams ran for Georgia governor in 2018 and 2022
But through the New Georgia Project and Fair Fight , organizations focused on engaging voters and protecting voting rights, she helped build an electorate that could imagine Georgia differently
She registered voters, challenged barriers to participation , and refused to accept that the South’s political future was fixed
Supporters listen as Democratic gubernatorial candidate Stacey Abrams speaks at a rally in Atlanta, Ga., on Nov. 5, 2022
Nathan Posner/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images And now another Black woman has won the office Abrams twice sought, in the third gubernatorial race in a row headed by a Black Democratic woman
There is something biblical about the path Abrams steadfastly cleared
I think of Moses, guiding his people toward the Promised Land but never entering it himself
Nor should her accomplishments be measured by another woman’s victory
But I believe there is sacred work in preparing a future you may never personally enjoy
And as a scholar of Black media history , I can reach even further back, to another woman who understood the audacity of claiming political power: Charlotta Bass

title: Young people turned out in near-record numbers for the 2026 midterms, with the economy top of their minds

<title>Young people turned out in near-record numbers for the 2026 midterms, with the economy top of their minds</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770377/original/file-20261105-64-cxj89m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C39%2C5233%2C3488&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A near record-high number of young people turned out to vote in the 2026 midterm elections. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/jackson-state-university-students-pose-with-tiger-voter-and-news-photo/2303391215?phrase=voting%20college%20students&amp;adppopup=true">Aron Smith/Jackson State University via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c39wz0970eypo">economy was the top issue</a> for voters in the November 2026 midterm elections, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/elections/voter-trends-national.html">which saw Democrats win decisive majorities</a> in both houses of Congress. </p>

<p>And for young voters, whether in college or not, the economy and jobs, as well as healthcare, were their top concerns, <a href="https://circle.tufts.edu/">our research at CIRCLE</a>, a nonpartisan, research organization focused on youth civic engagement at Tufts University, shows. </p>

<p>Overall, <a href="https://circle.tufts.edu/latest-research/2026-youth-voter-turnout-second-highest-last-30-years">27% of young people</a> – meaning people ages 18 to 29 – went to the polls during the midterms, our Nov. 5 analysis shows. This marks the second-highest midterm youth voter turnout in the past 30 years, behind only the 2018 election cycle. </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://tischcollege.tufts.edu/people/faculty/sara-suzuki">scholar at CIRCLE who studies young people</a> and their voting behavior, I think it’s helpful to understand some of the factors that motivated so many young people to vote – and to cast their lot with the Democrats.</p>

<h2>Understanding young voters</h2>

<p>Among youth, being enrolled as a college student or not did not make a big difference in who they voted for during these midterms. </p>

<p>But there are some voting trend differences based on young people’s educational attainment, especially in the gap between young people with an education level of high school or less, and those with at least some college experience and more. Those with only a high school degree or less voted Democratic by a 24-point margin, compared with a 42-point margin among those with at least some college education.</p>

<p>College students who are young men also <a href="https://circle.tufts.edu/2026-election">voted Democrat by a 24-point margin</a>. Female college students, meanwhile, voted Democrat at a 45-point margin. A similar gender gap appears among young voters who aren’t in college. </p>

<p>Overall, this gender gap has persisted at least since 2024, as young women then were also voting more Democratic than men were. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770373/original/file-20261105-64-7k0icp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A group of people are seen from behind, looking over tables that have white dividers on them." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770373/original/file-20261105-64-7k0icp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770373/original/file-20261105-64-7k0icp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770373/original/file-20261105-64-7k0icp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770373/original/file-20261105-64-7k0icp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770373/original/file-20261105-64-7k0icp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770373/original/file-20261105-64-7k0icp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770373/original/file-20261105-64-7k0icp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">People vote on Nov. 3, 2026, at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/people-vote-on-election-day-during-the-midterm-elections-at-news-photo/2302927132?phrase=voting%20college%20students&amp;adppopup=true">Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Latest youth voter trends</h2>

<p>About 66% of young people ages 18-29 voted for a Democratic candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives, compared with 31% for a Republican candidate, our data shows. This marks the highest percentage of support for Democratic candidates among all age groups.</p>

<p>Within this group, 70% of young women voted for a Democratic U.S. House candidate in the midterms, as opposed to 59% of young men. </p>

<p>Partisan trends among young voters have fluctuated over the past few decades – in 2000, for example, 49% of young people voted Democratic, while 48% voted Republican. </p>

<p>In 2026, Asian American and Pacific Islander, Black and Latino young people gave Democrat candidates the strongest support, at 81%, 79% and 71%, respectively. By comparison, 61% of white young people voted for Democratic House candidates, with 36% voting Republican. </p>

<h2>Young people are focused on the economy</h2>

<p>Across race, education, income and geographic location, young people overwhelmingly indicated that the economy and jobs was their top issue in this election. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.kff.org/public-opinion/health-care-in-the-2026-midterm-election/?entry=table-of-contents-key-takeaways">Healthcare</a> <a href="https://instituteforglobalaffairs.org/2026/09/is-the-iran-war-turning-young-voters-away-from-republicans-ahead-of-the-midterms/">and the Iran war</a> also showed up as areas of importance for young voters. <a href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/716333/issues-voters-say-matter-midterm.aspx">All three of these issues</a> are connected to young people’s concerns about the cost of living.  </p>

<p>We found that voting preferences did vary according to how young people viewed their own financial circumstances, a pattern that held among college students.  </p>

<p>Low-income students were more likely than their affluent peers <a href="https://circle.tufts.edu/latest-research/2026-youth-voter-turnout-second-highest-last-30-years">to vote for Democrats</a>. </p>

<p>The issues that matter most to young people have shifted considerably over the past several years.</p>

<p>In 2020, we were seeing different groups of young people prioritize <a href="https://circle.tufts.edu/latest-research/election-week-2020#the-top-issues-that-drove-youth-to-the-polls">social issues like racism</a>, climate change and gun control.</p>

<p>In 2022, we began to see <a href="https://circle.tufts.edu/2022-election-center#abortion-was-young-voters&amp;%23039;-top-issue-in-2022">young people prioritize the economy</a> – their concern about inflation was the second-most important issue to them after abortion. </p>

<p>Now, <a href="https://circle.tufts.edu/2024-election#economy-was-the-top-youth-issue,-drove-youth-vote-for-trump">after the economy</a>, healthcare was ranked second for young voters. The third-most important issue was the war in Iran. This is striking, because in the past, we’ve polled young voters about foreign policy issues like the war between Israel and Palestinians and the war between Russia and Ukraine. Young people have never really ranked these other foreign policy issues as a top area of concern. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770375/original/file-20261105-64-stso6t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A group of young people look beyond the camera and hold up blue signs that say 'Get out the early vote.'" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770375/original/file-20261105-64-stso6t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770375/original/file-20261105-64-stso6t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770375/original/file-20261105-64-stso6t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770375/original/file-20261105-64-stso6t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770375/original/file-20261105-64-stso6t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770375/original/file-20261105-64-stso6t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770375/original/file-20261105-64-stso6t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Students listen during a Democratic get-out-the-vote rally on the University of Wisconsin–Madison campus on Oct. 20, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/students-listen-as-wisconsin-democratic-gubernatorial-news-photo/2301205354?phrase=voting%20college%20students&amp;adppopup=true">Scott Olson/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>On the sidelines</h2>

<p>Youth voter turnout generally tends to be much weaker in midterm elections than in presidential elections. In 2018, there <a href="https://circle.tufts.edu/latest-research/28-young-people-voted-2018">was 28% turnout for young people</a> – a midterm turnout that was considerably higher than 2014, when only 13% of young people turned out to vote. </p>

<p>Campaigns seem to recognize that young voters tend to be less politically engaged. For example, our research shows that during the 2024 presidential election cycle, more than 1 in 3 young people were never contacted about the election. Among those <a href="https://circle.tufts.edu/latest-research/2024-poll-barriers-issues-economy">without college experience, 48% were never</a> contacted. </p>

<p>Our research still shows that college students <a href="https://circle.tufts.edu/latest-research/barriers-and-hardships-why-some-youth-didnt-vote-2024">face logistical barriers</a> to voting. </p>

<p>Young people are frequent movers, which means they might need to reregister whenever they change addresses. The fact that college students may be living on campus while they’re registered to vote from their parents’ address can also create complications. </p>

<p>College students <a href="https://circle.tufts.edu/latest-research/views-and-needs-college-students-ahead-2026-election">still have more voting information</a> than young people who are not in college. But compared with other age groups, young people receive less voting information – making their turnout in the 2026 midterms all the more remarkable.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295947/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>What C.S. Lewis said about Narnia’s most famous character: the Jesus-like lion Aslan</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770366/original/file-20261105-64-yw5kri.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3840%2C2560&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Many Christian readers appreciate the parallels between &#39;The Chronicles of Narnia&#39; and biblical stories.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Books-bookshelf-bookstore-159778.jpg">MorningbirdPhoto/Pixabay via Wikimedia Commons</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>As Netflix <a href="https://www.empireonline.com/movies/news/narnia-magicians-nephew-greta-gerwig-rock-opera-fantasy-bowie-exclusive/">teases glimpses</a> of <a href="https://www.netflix.com/tudum/videos/narnia-the-magicians-nephew-trailer">Greta Gerwig’s newest project</a>, an adaptation of <a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/narnia-the-magicians-nephew-movie-tie-in-paperback-c-s-lewis?variant=44866192900130">C.S. Lewis’ novel</a> “The Magician’s Nephew,” <a href="https://www.change.org/p/demand-netflix-to-replace-director-of-the-narnia-films">many Narnia fans</a> <a href="https://cfc.sebts.edu/apologetics-and-culture/aslan-gerwig-and-the-question-lewis-already-answered/">are worried</a>. In particular, there’s been online chatter about the new film’s depiction of the great lion Aslan: Will he <a href="https://variety.com/2026/film/news/greta-gerwig-narnia-david-bowie-meryl-streep-aslan-1236865755/">really look like David Bowie</a>, with <a href="https://deadline.com/2026/09/greta-gerwig-chose-meryl-streep-voice-aslan-narnia-1237107096/">the voice of Meryl Streep</a>?</p>

<p>For many readers, Aslan is not just a literary character, nor an ordinary hero: <a href="https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/thinking-about-aslan-and-jesus-with-c-s-lewis/">He is a representation of Jesus</a>. Aslan sings the entire world of Narnia into existence and performs Christ-like acts throughout Lewis’ “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-chronicles-of-narnia-deluxe-edition-c-s-lewis?variant=43406930346018">Chronicles of Narnia</a>,” which have sold over <a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/newsround/66938035">120 million copies worldwide</a> since the series’ publication in the 1950s.</p>



<p>As a scholar of medieval history and literature, I’ve taught and written about Lewis and <a href="https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/contributor/christopher-a-snyder/">“Lord of the Rings” author J.R.R. Tolkien</a>, who were close friends and colleagues for more than 30 years. Lewis himself <a href="https://www.english.ox.ac.uk/article/c.-s.-lewiss-oxford">was a medievalist at Oxford</a>, and both of their popular literary series are steeped in their knowledge of medieval languages, literature, mythology and theology. </p>

<p>Both authors acknowledged <a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-letters-of-jrr-tolkien-jrr-tolkien?variant=41069561872418">the ethical and religious themes of their fiction</a>. Yet Lewis rejected the idea that “The Chronicles” were simply an allegory. </p>

<h2>‘True myth’</h2>

<p>“<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-magicians-nephew-c-s-lewisc-s-lewis?variant=41143160340514">The Magician’s Nephew</a>,” published in 1955, was actually the last book in the series to be completed. Yet it serves as a prequel, narrating the creation of Narnia and the first appearance of its legitimate ruler, Aslan – the Turkish word for “lion.” </p>

<p>Later in the series, <a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-lion-the-witch-and-the-wardrobe-full-color-collectors-edition-c-s-lewis?variant=43128337104930">Aslan sacrifices himself</a> to save a young British boy, Edmund Pevensie, from the White Witch, Jadis. Aslan is resurrected through his knowledge of “deeper magic,” and royal power passes to the four Pevensie children.</p>

<p>Christian readers have long seen the series as an imaginative retelling of events from the Gospels, intended for children but offering much to adult readers as well. Critics like <a href="https://aeon.co/essays/a-rare-interview-with-philip-pullman-the-religious-atheist">Philip Pullman</a>, who wrote the 1990s fantasy trilogy “His Dark Materials,” <a href="https://www.bbc.com/videos/c8881qqw9w6o">have denounced “The Chronicles” as religious “propaganda</a>.”</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Adding to the book’s religious appeal was Lewis’ own very public faith. An atheist since his youth, he returned to worshipping in the Church of England after a <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/843035502">famous late-night conversation</a> with Tolkien in September 1931. </p>

<p>The two English professors had bonded over their interest in Norse myths, which Lewis called beautiful “lies breathed through silver.” For the devoutly Catholic Tolkien, however, ancient myths pointed to truths, not lies, and ultimately to the Gospels. He and other Christian friends at Oxford helped Lewis come to <a href="https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/blogs/evangelical-history/85-years-ago-today-j-r-r-tolkien-convinces-c-s-lewis-that-christ-is-the-true-myth/">accept Christianity as the “true myth.”</a></p>

<p>Almost immediately, Lewis began writing <a href="https://theocca.org/what-is-apologetics-defined/">Christian apologetics</a>, intellectual defenses of his faith, as well as fiction infused with Christian symbolism and theology. In 1947, he appeared on <a href="https://content.time.com/time/covers/0,16641,19470908,00.html">the cover of Time magazine</a> – well on his way to becoming arguably the most famous Christian apologist of the 20th century.</p>

<h2>‘Supposals’</h2>

<p>But what did Lewis himself say about Aslan?</p>

<p><a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-collected-letters-of-cs-lewis-volume-3-c-s-lewis?variant=32115116867618">His letters</a> and scholarly work indicate that “The Chronicles” were not meant to be <a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/education/glossary/allegory">allegorical</a>. In other words, Aslan was not simply a stand-in for Jesus, and the series was not an extended metaphor.</p>

<p>Rather, Lewis called the books “supposals:” a way of asking, “What if?”</p>

<p>Aslan gives “an imaginary answer to the question, ‘What might Christ become like if there really were a world like Narnia and He chose to be incarnate and die and rise again in that world as He actually has done in ours?” Lewis <a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-collected-letters-of-cs-lewis-volume-3-c-s-lewis?variant=32115116867618">wrote in a 1958 letter</a>. “This is not allegory at all.”</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769914/original/file-20261104-64-hmom3p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A black and white portrait of a serious-looking man in a suit jacket and tie." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769914/original/file-20261104-64-hmom3p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769914/original/file-20261104-64-hmom3p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=800&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769914/original/file-20261104-64-hmom3p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=800&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769914/original/file-20261104-64-hmom3p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=800&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769914/original/file-20261104-64-hmom3p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1005&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769914/original/file-20261104-64-hmom3p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1005&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769914/original/file-20261104-64-hmom3p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1005&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<p>Neither Lewis <a href="https://queerandback.substack.com/p/is-the-lord-of-the-rings-an-allegory">nor Tolkien</a> approved of easy allegorical readings of their fiction. Both professors argued that imaginative literature was <a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-personal-heresy-c-s-lewisemw-tillyard?variant=32116603715618">not simply the product of the author and their time</a>, a sealed treasure waiting for a biographical key to unlock its meaning. </p>

<p>And both men knew formal allegory quite well. Lewis’ 1936 book “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-allegory-of-love-c-s-lewis?variant=32132772823074">The Allegory of Love</a>” established his reputation as a critic of medieval and Renaissance literature. His 1933 novel “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-pilgrims-regress-c-s-lewis?variant=32115469582370">The Pilgrim’s Regress</a>” was an allegorical exploration of his own conversion, with characters that personified various abstract concepts and ideologies.</p>

<p>Tolkien wrote the allegorical short story “<a href="https://www.tolkienestate.com/writing/nadia-drici-leaf-by-niggle-the-peculiar-tale-of-a-painter-who-liked-to-draw-trees/">Leaf by Niggle</a>” as a way to explore his own doubts about ever finishing “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-lord-of-the-rings-deluxe-edition-jrr-tolkien?variant=39934965645346&amp;country=US&amp;currency=USD&amp;utm_medium=product_sync&amp;utm_source=google&amp;utm_content=sag_organic&amp;utm_campaign=sag_organic&amp;srsltid=AU7gw4UABIfUoviatlBqYfBHJTS3zRMJdqG3tSw9DSTCldiZG2HbziHGkdM">The Lord of the Rings</a>.” Like his earlier novel “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-hobbit-collectors-edition-j-r-r-tolkien?variant=41333552709666">The Hobbit</a>,” “The Lord of the Rings” only came to fruition through Lewis’ constant encouragement.</p>

<p>Narnia came to Lewis’ mind in bits and pieces. During World War II, when he took young evacuees from bombed cities into his home, a lion had haunted his dreams. A few other mental pictures came to him – a faun carrying packages, a lamppost in the snow – and he began writing. Aslan “just insisted on behaving in His own way,” Lewis later <a href="https://www.memoriapress.com/curriculum/mcp/c-s-lewis-letters-to-children/?srsltid=AYCX9vKX9zTgh7B3ob43RreZwUGz3DvXiVQzg1nD2fDsorGcPc1ko3rO">wrote to one schoolgirl</a>.</p>

<p>“The Chronicles” were not an allegory, he insisted, but symbolic. As he described in “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-allegory-of-love-c-s-lewis?variant=32132772823074">The Allegory of Love</a>,” “The symbolist leaves the given [facts] to find that which is more real.” Myth and symbols can, if used correctly, point to philosophical or theological truths more effectively than realistic fiction, making their created worlds feel more real. </p>

<h2>Scrutiny – and virtue</h2>

<p>For fans of “The Chronicles,” Narnia feels “real” in this sense – an escape to truth, rather than an escape from truth. Adapting these stories to film, however, always runs the risk of moving further away from what Lewis captured so brilliantly in his prose.</p>

<p>In 2018, the author’s estate <a href="https://www.rollingstone.com/tv-movies/tv-movie-news/netflix-chronicles-of-narnia-732500/">sold Netflix the rights</a> to adapt the book series to screen, and Gerwig was later tapped to write and direct at least two Narnia films. Douglas Gresham, one of Lewis’ stepsons, has an executive producer credit on “<a href="https://www.netflix.com/tudum/articles/narnia-release-date">Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew</a>,” and <a href="https://www.narniaweb.com/2026/10/c-s-lewis-family-releases-official-statement-on-narnia-the-magicians-nephew/">has generally been enthusiastic</a> about the project. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/gDJ-ini7fF0?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">‘The Magician’s Nephew’ is scheduled to arrive on Feb. 12, 2027.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Gerwig herself has expressed <a href="https://www.narniaweb.com/everything-greta-gerwig-has-said-about-netflixs-narnia-movies/">her “reverence” for Lewis’ work</a>. “It was the book of my childhood,” she <a href="https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/business/story/2026-03-19/netflix-upcoming-movies-2026">said at a press event</a> in 2024. “It was the book series that I loved, and I lived through, and I spent so much time imagining myself inside of Narnia.”</p>

<p>Intense scrutiny of the project should surprise no one. As with <a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt3281548/">her film “Little Women,”</a> Gerwig is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108589604">adapting a beloved novel</a>. And this time, it is a novel written by a very public atheist-turned-Christian whose works have <a href="https://www.cslewisinstitute.org/resources/a-biography-of-mere-christianity/">inspired the faith</a> of countless others. Still, her “Magician’s Nephew” should not be judged by a trailer and a handful of interviews.</p>

<p>Lewis likely never expected that “The Chronicles” would turn into a live-action film, but he did believe in the power of imaginative art – whether ancient, medieval or modern – to move one toward truth. The virtues Faith, Hope, Charity and Prudence are frequently depicted in the <a href="https://www.ivpress.com/the-medieval-mind-of-c-s-lewis?srsltid=ARcRdnoUO4va5ZJV6b7t_UFnt6Vrbl95ek6XYDWGDR3VyyEj-iJvzMHk">medieval</a> and <a href="https://anunexpectedjournal.com/the-virtuous-arthur/">Renaissance literature</a> that Lewis loved and taught. Fans and filmmaker alike might benefit from remembering these virtues as well.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294140/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>I’m an athletic trainer – here’s how to know when kids sports are too intense</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766058/original/file-20261014-50-f6e2hj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5130%2C3420&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">More isn&#39;t always better when it comes to training in youth sports. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/little-league-team-cheering-royalty-free-image/56901647">Ariel Skelley/DigitalVision via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>At a recent T-ball game, I was talking with another father who mentioned that his son had never played before. As we watched our children falling over trying to scoop up a ground ball, we laughed about how they were still figuring everything out. There was something refreshing about seeing kids learn a game without worrying about how well they were playing.</p>

<p>That moment stayed with me. I’ve spent years as an athletic trainer in collegiate and professional sports, helping athletes stay healthy, handle the demands of competition and perform at their best. Today, I’m a <a href="https://www.uta.edu/academics/faculty/profile?user=adam.annaccone">clinical associate professor of kinesiology and chief health and performance adviser</a> for an NCAA Division I athletics program. Given my work, you might expect me to take an active role in developing my own children’s athletic abilities, especially in a youth sports culture where early specialization and greater commitment are often seen as advantages. </p>

<p>And I understand the appeal. Like any parent, I want my children to have opportunities, and it’s easy to wonder whether another practice or lesson might help them get ahead. But with twins who are nearly 6, I’m more interested in whether they enjoy sports than how good they become at them. </p>

<p>As they get older, particularly if they want to pursue sports seriously, my role as a parent will change. Right now, I can step back and let them explore. But as training and competition become more demanding, I’ll want to become more involved in understanding and questioning those demands. Research on training, recovery and athletic development can help parents navigate what’s appropriate as their children’s sports experiences intensify.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/uR9x0g2FbPk?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Experts recommend that children engage in a wide variety of physical activities before specializing in one sport.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Knowing when to step back</h2>

<p>When I’m watching my children play, I’d rather be their dad than their performance coach. When they ask to practice hitting or throwing, I’m happy to help. They usually decide when we’re done. Twenty minutes? Great. Five minutes? That’s fine too. </p>

<p>Practice matters, but giving children some control over when and how they practice can help keep it from becoming another obligation.</p>

<p>Research involving more than 9,000 young athletes found that children tend to be more motivated to participate in sports when parents support their ability to <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1291711">make decisions about their participation</a>.</p>

<p>As children get older, their goals may change. Some will want to compete at higher levels or focus on a particular sport. Those ambitions deserve support, but giving children a voice doesn’t mean parents should step away from important decisions. As commitments grow, parents may need to ask more questions about training schedules, recovery time and the expectations placed on their children.</p>



<h2>More isn’t always better</h2>

<p>I’ve heard parents describe traveling hours for youth sports tournaments, only to discover that many of the teams competing came from the same communities they had traveled from. One parent recalled driving to Houston for a tournament where six of the eight teams were from the Dallas-Fort Worth area.</p>

<p>I understand how families end up in these situations. An extra practice, private lessons or joining a more competitive team can each seem reasonable. Over time, those commitments become expectations, and saying no isn’t always easy when your child is part of a team.</p>

<p>But more training doesn’t automatically produce better athletes. My experience in sports medicine and performance has taught me that improvement depends on how athletes respond to training, not simply how much they do. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2015-094962">Training places demands on the body</a>, and athletes need time to adapt. </p>

<p>The American Academy of Pediatrics cautions that excessive training and early specialization are associated with <a href="https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2023-065129">increased overuse injury risk</a> and may contribute to burnout. Risk depends on training volume, recovery and individual development, particularly during adolescence.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767275/original/file-20261020-50-ii5r6a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Girls running a race on a track field." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767275/original/file-20261020-50-ii5r6a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767275/original/file-20261020-50-ii5r6a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767275/original/file-20261020-50-ii5r6a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767275/original/file-20261020-50-ii5r6a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767275/original/file-20261020-50-ii5r6a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767275/original/file-20261020-50-ii5r6a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767275/original/file-20261020-50-ii5r6a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Persistent soreness, unusual fatigue or declining enthusiasm can be a sign of burnout for kids in youth sports.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/schoolgirls-running-race-on-track-field-royalty-free-image/2192145273">Klaus Vedfelt/DigitalVision via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>As training demands increase, parents should pay attention to how their children are responding, not just whether they’re experiencing pain. Persistent fatigue, declining performance, changes in sleep or a loss of enthusiasm may suggest that recovery isn’t keeping pace with training. Even an athlete who loves their sport can reach a point where the demands become too much. These are reasons for a parent to discuss the workload with their child and coaches, while persistent or worsening pain warrants medical evaluation.</p>

<p>Athletic development also benefits from variety. Running, climbing, jumping and exploring different activities can help develop <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-024-05385-8">coordination and a range of movement skills</a>. The International Olympic Committee recommends <a href="https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2015-094962">varied physical activity</a> and developmentally appropriate training, including for children who may eventually specialize. </p>

<p>Just as important is whether young athletes want to keep playing. Children who enjoy sports are more likely to <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.871936">want to continue participating</a>, research shows. When young soccer players were asked <a href="https://doi.org/10.1123/jpah.2013-0180">what made sports fun</a>, they identified working hard, improving and spending time with teammates. Even the best training program won’t accomplish much if an athlete no longer wants to participate.</p>

<h2>Leaving the game at the field</h2>

<p>In collegiate and professional sports, reviewing performance is routine. After competition, staff identify what worked, what didn’t and what needs attention. But children don’t need a performance review every time they climb into the car.</p>

<p>I let my children start conversations about their games. If they want to talk about a missed ball, something funny or something that upset them, I’ll listen. If they want to talk about something else, that’s fine too.</p>

<p>Researchers who recorded parent-child car rides around sporting events found that much of the time passed in silence and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.psychsport.2021.102095">sports came up relatively infrequently</a>. They also observed occasions when parents interrupted or provided feedback before children could respond. The findings don’t establish one right way to handle the drive home, but they offer parents a reason to consider whether their children want feedback in the first place.</p>

<p>No parent knows whether their child will become a competitive athlete, play recreationally or eventually find interests outside organized sports. I’m comfortable leaving that future open for my children. As a father, I’m far more interested in whether my kids will want to play again next week than how well they played today.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293479/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
