<title>What the measles vaccine’s ‘97% effective’ rating means for Pittsburgh parents</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769637/original/file-20261102-64-euy56x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1024%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Demand for the MMR vaccine has risen in Pennsylvania as the state’s measles outbreak has grown.
</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/daniela-chavarriaga-holds-her-daughter-emma-chavarriaga-as-news-photo/495311875?phrase=measles+shot">Joe Raedle via Getty Images News</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Pennsylvania is experiencing its worst measles outbreak in more than three decades, with <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/diseases-conditions/infectious-disease/measles">more than 1,400 confirmed cases and six measles-associated deaths</a> so far in 2026, according to statistics compiled by the state.</p>

<p>Each new case brings a new warning of a measles exposure in that community. Exposures have occurred at <a href="https://www.alleghenycounty.us/News-Articles/Allegheny-County-Press-Releases/September-2026/9-1-26-ACHD-Potential-Measles-Exposure-Statement">hospitals and doctors’ offices</a>, <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/newsroom/doh-responding-to-two-separate-potential-measles-exposures-in-la">grocery stores</a> and <a href="https://www.wtae.com/article/travelers-potential-exposure-measles-pa-turnpike-westmoreland-county/73597055">restaurants</a>, and <a href="https://www.wpxi.com/news/local/measles-confirmed-allegheny-county-school/B6USNLCVWNCLXLZMFMKSETNE6I/">K-12 schools</a> and <a href="https://pennstatehealthnews.org/2026/10/penn-state-health-notifies-public-of-potential-measles-exposures-in-hershey-and-lancaster/">universities</a>. </p>

<p>Exposure alerts come with the same instructions: Check your MMR vaccine status, and watch for symptoms for the next three weeks. People are told that two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/vaccines/index.html">97% effective</a> at preventing measles. The underlying message is that if you’re vaccinated, you’re protected. </p>

<p>The MMR vaccine is highly effective at preventing disease, but it isn’t a guarantee. People may hear that 97% figure and wonder <a href="https://www.nfid.org/resource/frequently-asked-questions-about-measles/">about the other 3%</a>. </p>

<p>Parents ask me: Should I be worried? How do I know if my kid has measles? Do I need an MMR booster? Most recently, my teenage daughter texted me to ask about her MMR vaccine status. She was worried about what would happen if she were exposed. </p>

<p>These are questions I can answer as both a mother and an <a href="https://allegheny.edu/about/campus-department-resources/faculty-and-staff-directory/becky-dawson/">epidemiologist in northwestern Pennsylvania</a>. I became both at once. My daughter was born at the start of my doctoral program, and I read epidemiology textbooks aloud to her while studying for my comprehensive exams. I defended my dissertation on my son’s due date. I’m a better mother because I’m an epidemiologist, and a better epidemiologist because I’m a mom. </p>

<h2>Are these measles exposure alerts cause for alarm?</h2>

<p>The advice in each public measles exposure alert <a href="https://www.chop.edu/clinical-pathway/suspected-measles-exposure-infection-clinical-pathway">matches the guidance doctors follow</a> when a patient may have been exposed.</p>

<p>Everyone is asked to <a href="https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/health/documents/topics/documents/diseases-and-conditions/Measles.pdf">watch for symptoms</a>, whether or not they’re vaccinated. The number of unvaccinated people across Pennsylvania <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2026.22533">is growing</a>. As a result, <a href="https://www.alleghenycounty.us/files/assets/county/v/4/government/health/documents/vaccine-coverage/2025-to-2026-immunization-report.pdf">many communities</a>, including Allegheny County, no longer have herd immunity. </p>

<p>Four of the over 1,400 confirmed measles cases in Pennsylvania were <a href="https://www.wgal.com/article/pennsylvania-measles-four-vaccinated-people-test-positive/73690629">people who had been vaccinated</a>. These cases are known as <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/measles-breakthrough-infections-causes-vaccine-symptoms-rcna201799">breakthrough infections</a>. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769639/original/file-20261102-64-4my5df.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A sign informs patients of a pop-up measles vaccination clinic." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769639/original/file-20261102-64-4my5df.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769639/original/file-20261102-64-4my5df.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769639/original/file-20261102-64-4my5df.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769639/original/file-20261102-64-4my5df.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769639/original/file-20261102-64-4my5df.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769639/original/file-20261102-64-4my5df.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769639/original/file-20261102-64-4my5df.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Pop-up clinics in Pennsylvania have offered MMR vaccines as the state’s measles outbreak grows.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/sign-outside-a-mobile-clinic-offering-measles-and-flu-news-photo/2259641016?phrase=pop%20up%20vaccination%20clinic%20measles&amp;adppopup=true">Sean Rayford/Stringer via Getty Images News</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The term “herd immunity” wasn’t <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(20)31924-3">coined until 1918</a>. That year, a veterinarian wrote about an outbreak of “contagious abortion” in sheep and cattle, a literal herd. Today, herd immunity means that the risk of disease for susceptible people, those without immunity, drops when they are surrounded by people who are immune. </p>

<p>In other words, if the people around you are immune, you’re unlikely to get sick even if you’re susceptible. For measles, that protection depends on about 95% of people being immune. In a school or community where fewer than 95% of people are vaccinated, measles can spread more easily. </p>

<p>In Allegheny County, <a href="https://www.theprogressnews.com/health-directors-say-pittsburgh-region-is-well-protected-from-measles-but-obstacles-remain/article_51d88aa3-9279-4e08-ad0c-937eed2966fb.html">93.8% of children are fully vaccinated against measles</a>. Some neighborhoods are above 97% uptake, while others are <a href="https://www.pghcitypaper.com/news-2/health/immunization-rates-lag-at-some-greater-pittsburgh-schools-as-measles-spreads-in-pennsylvania/">below the necessary 95% needed for herd immunity</a>. </p>

<h2>What happens after an exposure?</h2>

<p>Measles exposures are announced publicly by the <a href="https://www.pa.gov/governor/newsroom/2026-press-releases/shapiro-administration-expands-measles-response-efforts">Department of Health</a> and <a href="https://www.mmchs.org/news/potential-measles-exposure-in-mmc-emergency-department/">local healthcare providers</a>. During a measles outbreak, public health departments may get in touch with close contacts to alert them to an exposure. </p>

<p>Public exposure alerts, like the one made in October after there was <a href="https://www.wtae.com/article/pennsylvania-measles-allegheny-county-target-exposure/74040205">a measles exposure at a Target near Pittsburgh</a>, are also used. Public alerts are for settings where exposed people can’t be identified and contacted individually. Measles is so contagious that a single case can infect <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/s1473-3099(17)30307-9">up to 18 susceptible people</a>.</p>

<p>Measles spreads through the air and through respiratory droplets, like those released when someone sneezes. The virus can also <a href="https://www.healthychildren.org/English/health-issues/vaccine-preventable-diseases/Pages/Measles.aspx">survive outside the body</a>, lingering in the air and on surfaces.</p>

<p>Imagine I have measles and walk into my local grocery store. I’m contagious from about four days before the rash appears until four days after. Every time I breathe out, I release virus particles into the air, and those particles can stay infectious for up to two hours. If I sneeze in the produce section, the virus can survive on surfaces for up to two hours.</p>



<p>However, if you’ve had measles or were vaccinated with two doses of the MMR vaccine, you are protected. Two doses <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/vaccines/index.html">provides 97% lifetime protection against measles</a>. This means that even without herd immunity, fewer than 3% of individuals with immunity are likely to contract measles. Adults who have had measles, or who have documentation of the recommended doses of the MMR vaccine, <a href="https://health.mit.edu/faqs/faq-measles#faq--4354">don’t need a booster</a>. </p>

<p>People who were vaccinated between 1963 and 1967, or who aren’t sure which vaccine they received, <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/do-adults-need-a-measles-booster-an-epidemiologist-explains-who-is-immune">should talk to their primary care provider</a> about whether they need another dose. This is because the measles vaccine used between those years <a href="https://www.yalemedicine.org/news/should-you-get-a-measles-vaccine-booster">was not as effective as the MMR vaccine that is currently given</a>. </p>

<p>Today, children typically get their first dose of the MMR vaccine at <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/downloads/mmr-recommendations-measles.pdf">12 to 15 months old and a second dose at 4 to 6 years old</a>. Because the vaccine is given in early childhood, people born in the early to mid-1960s are the most likely to have received the older vaccine. People born before 1957 are <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/pdf/rr/rr6204.pdf">generally considered immune</a>, because measles was so widespread then that almost everyone caught it as a child.</p>

<h2>What are the symptoms of measles?</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/measles/symptoms-causes/syc-20374857">Symptoms of measles</a> include a high fever that can reach 105 degrees Fahrenheit (40.6 degrees Celsius), a cough, a runny nose and conjunctivitis, also known as pin keye. These symptoms overlap with those of other respiratory viruses, such as flu and COVID-19.</p>

<p>Most people with measles develop a red, blotchy rash. It starts on the face and spreads down the body, <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/signs-symptoms/photos.html">like paint poured from a bucket</a>. People who are immunocompromised or were previously vaccinated, even with one dose of the MMR vaccine, may not develop the rash. Between <a href="https://www.ccjm.org/content/ccjom/77/3/207.full.pdf">25% and 40% of immunocompromised people with measles never get the rash</a>. </p>



<p>A telltale sign of measles is <a href="https://medlineplus.gov/ency/imagepages/2558.htm">Koplik spots</a>, tiny white spots inside the mouth that can show up a day or two before the rash. </p>

<h2>Why does measles keep making headlines?</h2>

<p>Measles can have serious consequences. About <a href="https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/257220">1 in 20 people</a> with measles develop pneumonia, and up to <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html">3 in 1,000 cases</a> end in death. <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/downloads/measlesdataandstatsslideset.pdf">Children younger than 5 and adults older than 20</a> are most likely to experience these severe complications.</p>

<p>Without herd immunity in many communities, measles cases, hospitalizations and deaths in Pennsylvania are likely to keep rising. The state Department of Health reports <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/diseases-conditions/infectious-disease/measles">community spread of measles in 14 of Pennsylvania’s 67 counties</a>.</p>

<p>Each of these cases is mostly preventable with the MMR vaccine. The U.S. declared measles <a href="https://www.kff.org/other-health/measles-elimination-status-what-it-is-and-how-the-u-s-could-lose-it/">eliminated in 2000</a>, meaning it was no longer spreading continuously here. This year’s outbreak shows how quickly that can change and the negative health consequences it can have in our communities.</p>

Pop-up clinics in Pennsylvania have offered MMR vaccines as the state’s measles outbreak grows
Sean Rayford/Stringer via Getty Images News The term “herd immunity” wasn’t coined until 1918
That year, a veterinarian wrote about an outbreak of “contagious abortion” in sheep and cattle, a literal herd
Today, herd immunity means that the risk of disease for susceptible people, those without immunity, drops when they are surrounded by people who are immune
In other words, if the people around you are immune, you’re unlikely to get sick even if you’re susceptible
For measles, that protection depends on about 95% of people being immune
In a school or community where fewer than 95% of people are vaccinated, measles can spread more easily
In Allegheny County, 93.8% of children are fully vaccinated against measles
Some neighborhoods are above 97% uptake, while others are below the necessary 95% needed for herd immunity
What happens after an exposure? Measles exposures are announced publicly by the Department of Health and local healthcare providers
During a measles outbreak, public health departments may get in touch with close contacts to alert them to an exposure
Public exposure alerts, like the one made in October after there was a measles exposure at a Target near Pittsburgh , are also used
Public alerts are for settings where exposed people can’t be identified and contacted individually
Measles is so contagious that a single case can infect up to 18 susceptible people
Measles spreads through the air and through respiratory droplets, like those released when someone sneezes
The virus can also survive outside the body , lingering in the air and on surfaces
Imagine I have measles and walk into my local grocery store
I’m contagious from about four days before the rash appears until four days after
Every time I breathe out, I release virus particles into the air, and those particles can stay infectious for up to two hours

title: Trump doubles down on everything that lost him the midterms
excerpt: Donald Trump speaks to reporters on Air Force One as Stephen Miller and Karoline Leavitt watch on July 29, 2025. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images This story appeare
body: Donald Trump speaks to reporters on Air Force One as Stephen Miller and Karoline Leavitt watch on July 29, 2025. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump is doubling down after a midterm annihilation.  What happened? On Friday afternoon, Trump announced that longtime aide Stephen Miller would take over as White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles

In a post to Truth Social, Trump said that Miller would start on Monday, but the change appears to be effective more or less immediately — Wiles has already resigned .  Why the change? Trump was reportedly angry with Wiles over the GOP’s collapse in the midterm elections, which saw Democrats winning up and down the ballot even in traditionally deep-red parts of the country.  Trump, for his part, told reporters on Friday that Wiles had “done a very good job.” But, he added, “we gotta make moves
Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.” What should I know about Miller? Miller is currently the White House deputy chief of staff for policy, as well as homeland security adviser

More importantly, he’s the architect and engine of some of Trump’s most vicious immigration policies, including family separation (during the first Trump term) and ICE’s current campaign of indiscriminate, militarized immigration enforcement.  He’s also an ally of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has to be feeling a little bit better about his imperiled job (though it won’t keep Hegseth from facing impeachment in the near future)
What does this mean for the Trump presidency? More of the same, cranked up to 11

Miller is as hardline as they come, and he’s certain to push Trump to be even more aggressive on immigration and attempts to use the machinery of government to attack their shared political enemies .  It’s all going to be extraordinarily unpopular, if Tuesday’s midterm results are anything to go by — but with just over two years left in the White House, there’s little reason to believe that Miller and Trump won’t try to push the power of the presidency to its breaking point

And with that, it’s time to log off… Let’s end the week on a high note with this piece from my colleague Christian Paz, who writes that “the decency was the point” for voters and Democratic candidates alike in the 2026 midterms
If you’d prefer something even lighter to head into the weekend, I also recommend the Smithsonian’s cheetah cam
Enjoy, have a great weekend, and we’ll see you on Monday!

title: A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure
excerpt: A sweeping new Senate bill aims to speed up the notoriously slow US energy permitting process—but whether it helps or hurts emissions depends entirely on what g
body: A sweeping new Senate bill aims to speed up the notoriously slow US energy permitting process—but whether it helps or hurts emissions depends entirely on what gets built
The bill's backers span the political spectrum, from the White House to clean energy groups, who argue renewables stand to win economically if more building is unlocked

Critics warn the bill could open the floodgates for fossil fuel expansion, with one modeler finding it may have actually increased energy sector emissions and air pollution risks had it been in place in 2025. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148062" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US
With the dust barely settled on this week’s momentous midterms, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on November 9
It’s a plan that could finally start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved, as part of something called permitting reform
People on both sides of the political aisle have been pushing for this type of change for some years

The key question is whether this will cut greenhouse-gas emissions from the US energy sector or push them higher still.   The federal permitting system is designed to protect the environment against industrial pollution from large projects like power plants, transmission lines, and natural-gas pipelines
Today, permitting is governed by a range of laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act
And if there’s one thing you might know about the current state of permitting in the US it’s that it’s slow and incredibly complicated
So in its 417 pages, BAAJA attempts to tighten things up

The bill has provisions that narrow the sorts of projects that need to apply for federal permits and others that enact deadlines in hopes of speeding up a process that today can take years. (There are also specific provisions about transmission planning, mining, and the rest of the kitchen sink; this thing is dense .) One thing to know about this bill is that it’s largely technology neutral: It opens the doors for the buildout of projects involving both fossil fuels and renewables
So there’s a weird mishmash of legislators and outside groups supporting it
The bill’s four sponsors in the Senate are two Republicans and two Democrats
The White House has backed this permitting reform bill, with its Council of Economic Advisors finding that it would reduce review times and have economic benefits like boosting GDP

Clean energy groups like the American Clean Power Association have largely come out in favor of the bill too, with the group’s analysis finding that it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid
Some environmental groups, however, oppose the bill, or parts of it

An assessment from the Natural Resources Defense Council says the parts about transmission could have substantial benefits for the grid, but the narrowing of environmental reviews could be damaging for public and private lands
Many in the climate world have long been calling for permitting reform, arguing that renewables stand to benefit more than fossil fuels
The thinking is that solar and wind power are some of the cheapest sources available today, so if we unlock the ability to build more energy, they are likely to win out economically
A few early analyses have tried to quantify just what BAAJA would mean for emissions in the US

One, from the think tank Rhodium Group, found that in the best-case scenario, the bill would cut economy-wide emissions by 4%, reduce annual energy bills by $78 per household, and add 200 gigawatts of new clean energy by 2040
In the worst case, emissions would stay about the same

Another report , from the nonprofit research group Resources for the Future, found that the bill could cut power-sector emissions 6% by 2041 and save more than $350 billion on system costs by midcentury
But there are some concerns that this permitting bill’s real effect would be to open the floodgates for new natural-gas plants

As data centers have put more pressure on the grid, a wave of such plants have been announced. “You get down to a trade-off between essentially growing the clean electricity industry on the one hand and then, as a compromise, growing the fossil-fuel industry on the other,” says Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue

To quantify that trade-off, Kircher also modeled the potential emissions effects of the bill and found that if BAAJA had been in place in 2025, energy sector emissions would have been higher than the actual baseline
Health and mortality risks associated with air pollution would also have increased
This bill is scheduled for a Senate vote on November 9, well before the next Congress takes control
It’s not clear what the dramatic victories for Democrats might mean for the legislation, which was expected to pass the Senate with largely Republican support if a few Democrats got on board
Democrats could decide to wait for next year, when they’ll have control of both chambers

But any deal would ultimately need to win Trump’s signature, limiting what a future bill might be able to change.  In a world where permitting new projects is easier, we’ll see more clean energy, but we’ll see more natural gas, too
And while prices could get lower, that could push demand for electricity higher, leading to more emissions overall
Simplifying the permitting system and cutting red tape is a worthy goal
But when it comes to emissions, it still really matters what, exactly, you want to build.

title: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
excerpt: Texas's data center boom may be over: Texas has been the fastest-growing data center market in the US, but a Democratic sweep of the governor's mansio
body: Texas's data center boom may be over: Texas has been the fastest-growing data center market in the US, but a Democratic sweep of the governor's mansion and Senate seat—with candidates who campaigned hard against data centers—has the industry bracing for moratoriums and permit freezes

The projects at stake are enormous: Two facilities alone—Stargate Frontier and Nexus Hubbard—represent thousands of megawatts of planned AI infrastructure, making any slowdown a serious blow to Big Tech's ambitions and the broader economy

Voters sent a clear message: Across the US, midterm voters backed efforts to shield ratepayers from data center-driven electricity costs and supported outright bans on new facilities—a sign that Big Tech has badly failed to convince the public that AI will actually improve their lives

Governing is harder than campaigning: Local officials, complicated county-by-county politics, and construction unions that backed Democratic candidates could all complicate any push for a sweeping moratorium. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148043" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts
But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position
Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton
Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott
At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years
Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail
Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing
At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September

That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities , began changing course himself.  Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails
On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits
Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether.  The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that
Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium
That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state
The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive

The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas

Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.  The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall
Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back
And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects
Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices
Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether

If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it

A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere.  It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas
Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton
Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift

But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red.  This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted

Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices.  Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state
And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns

So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.
